They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.

items.title: Examining form-based linguistic productivity in people and large language models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linguistic productivity, as evidenced by the use of words in novel contexts, is one of the most striking facts about human language. However, how abstract the knowledge that enables such productivity is remains unclear. We compare people's and computational language models' linguistic productivity in contexts where successful generalization depends on form-based information. We focus on extending the use of a novel verb learned in the active voice to passive contexts. We find people extend active to passive uses in a way consistent with abstract generalizations concerning linguistic form, even when no plausible meaning can be assigned to the novel verb. In contrast, large language models succeeded only when a meaning like an existing verb's could be assigned to the novel verb. We conclude that computational models' syntactic knowledge remains tied to the distribution and meaning of specific lexical items in a way that human syntactic knowledge is not.

items.title: Style over Substance? Linguistic Bias in LLM-based Peer Review
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35254v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The number of paper submissions to major AI conferences has increased dramatically in recent years, substantially increasing the peer-review workload of researchers. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support peer review, both by individual reviewers and by conference organizations. While LLM capabilities have improved considerably, their evaluations may be influenced by linguistic characteristics that are unrelated to scientific content. In this work, we introduce a controlled experimental framework for studying such effects by systematically perturbing the linguistic style of research papers. Specifically, we rewrite papers to exhibit (i) linguistic features associated with native or non-native English writing, and (ii) high- or low-confidence linguistic features. To construct these interventions, we derive fine-grained rewriting instructions grounded in the linguistic literature and apply them using LLMs. Crucially, our interventions are designed to preserve the underlying scientific content. We then evaluate the resulting papers using different LLM reviewers. Our experiments expose a critical vulnerability in LLM-based peer review: reviewers systematically reward confident rhetoric independent of scientific content, raising serious concerns about the robustness of their assessments.

items.title: CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36734v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.

items.title: Illusory Truth or Salient Anomaly? Model-Dependent Responses to Repeated Poisoned Passages in RAG-Style Contexts
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41012v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repeated passages in retrieved evidence may influence how language models identify misinformation, even when those passages restate a single underlying claim rather than provide independent support. We compare four instruction-tuned models on 200 claims from the BEIR SciFact test split using paired, fixed seven-document contexts. The minority condition contains one poisoned document and six non-target documents, whereas the majority condition contains the original poisoned document, five paraphrases, and one non-target document. Poison detection rates increase from 45.5% to 66.0% for Apertus-8B and from 4.0% to 15.5% for Aya-Expanse-8B, but decrease from 80.0% to 47.5% for Mistral-Nemo and from 25.0% to 9.5% for Gemma-3-12B-IT. All four paired comparisons are statistically significant. These contrasting results suggest that repeated poisoned evidence does not affect all models in the same way. One possible interpretation is that repetition makes the poisoned claim more conspicuous to some models, potentially facilitating its detection, while other models may treat repeated formulations as reinforcing evidence, potentially reducing their ability to identify the poisoned claim. Although these interpretations require further investigation, the findings highlight the importance of model-dependent responses to repeated evidence in retrieval-augmented settings.

items.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41291v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 12.3 to 194.9 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

items.title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.00911v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decision-making in humans and AI involves multiple cognitive abilities. System One decision models produce fast, structured choices. Their cognitive strengths and limitations, however, remain poorly understood. We introduce S1CogBench, a benchmark of 24 established cognitive tasks and 27 evaluation modes, evaluating seven open models and the API model Jev. It combines human-response prediction, autonomous execution, and controlled task manipulations to reveal strengths and failures that aggregate scores miss. We find distinct behavioral profiles across the evaluated models. In these models, strong performance on some learning tasks coexists with failures to gather information or adapt to feedback, while high accuracy does not guarantee human-like responses to changing task demands. Shared readout controls show that model rankings depend partly on how choices are extracted. Separate latency comparisons with generative language models show that long responses are much slower than direct decisions, whereas matched one-token generation adds little overhead. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments. It provides a common empirical basis for identifying their capabilities and limitations before integrating them into automated decision systems.

items.title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01519v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.

items.title: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains
items.summary: arXiv:2611.03576v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Law changes over time. A court decides a case under the law in force on that day, and legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law. We checked 156,650 decisions of four Thai courts. Up to 67% of them cite law that has since been amended or repealed. We introduce Nitibench+, the sequel of our NitiBench, a Thai legal QA benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it holds both the text in force on the decision date and the current text, and its retrieval corpus holds every dated version of every Thai statute section. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric, the Bar-standard score, and on the overlap between the cited sections and the court's. The report has two parts. Part I measures the cost of the wrong text on 13 open-weight models. Reading the current text of amended law drops the Bar-standard score by 0.25 and missing repealed law drops it by 0.79. The penalty comes from rule changes, 0.45 on the 428 rule-changed items and none on the 331 wording-only items, and Citation F1 does not see it. The text in force is the fair setting. Part II benchmarks today's models on that setting. A public leaderboard ranks 33 models on a held-out test split of 500 items stratified by domain, with a validation split of the same shape released for public use, from memory alone, with the court's sections provided, and as a retrieval agent over the law in force, with the cost per item and the hallucinated citations. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool only five open-weight models recall any Thai law, and with it 27 of the 33 models gain and six lose. Leaderboard will take new models as they are released. Legal benchmarks must track dates, and on the right text today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law.

items.title: Discourse Analysis of Legislative Bill Discussions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05381v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Legislative hearings are distinct communication events with their own human recognizable structure and logic, yet they have been analyzed as distinct phenomena beyond their transcripts. Understanding legislative hearings at a deeper level is a major step in analyzing the work and power relationships within democratic bodies. In this work, we present a novel end-to-end pipeline for parsing rhetorical structures from legislative committee hearings with the goal of improving legislative discourse analysis and democratic accountability. We also propose a rhetorical structure grammar and find that 74.71% of California state bill discussions in our dataset can be parsed with this grammar. We evaluate our pipeline with two utterance section classifiers on a random subset of over 2619 annotated utterances corresponding to 100 hearings. We find that a logistic regression-based classifier with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing outperforms more complex models, achieving an F1 score of 59.0% against our ground truth discourse section labels.

items.title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07940v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage. Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC. Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%. Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

items.title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08439v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, checked for overlap with the training data. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24. Several of these gains rest partly on one label that the earlier release almost never chose; fitting one bias per option removes part of them, while the jargon gain largely survives. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: its loss on 17 abbreviations unrelated to training (-0.060) is one label and disappears after the same correction. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation, and the earlier recipe varies across seeds by up to 0.098 on the strictest slice. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points, narrowed to -3.4 and +1.4 by the per-option biases; a second training run of each recipe, the augmented one under a rule recorded beforehand, puts the recipe gap on jargon far above seed noise and on a third unseen dataset, scientific rubrics, only just above it. Rankings of training checkpoints disagree across the three unseen datasets, so none of them should choose the checkpoint. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

Rankings of training checkpoints disagree across the three unseen datasets, so none of them should choose the checkpoint. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

items.title: Beyond Truncation: When Can LLMs Safely Omit Generated Text?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08975v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.

items.title: Understanding When and Where Self-Supervised Speech Models Learn Phonemes and Prosodic Cues through Layer-Wise and Time-Resolved Probing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.11249v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) encode a rich hierarchy of acoustic, prosodic, and phonetic information, yet when and where it emerges during pretraining remains unclear. We train frozen-encoder probes on every Transformer layer across pretraining checkpoints of two matched models: HuBERT-Base, whose stage 2 is a separately initialized model trained on new pseudo-label targets, and single-objective wav2vec 2.0-Base. Our five tasks span an acoustic-to-abstract gradient: absolute pitch (F0), speaker-relative pitch, lexical stress, phoneme boundaries, and 38-way phoneme identity. Acoustic-prosodic cues and phone boundaries are decodable from the earliest checkpoints and barely shift across layers, whereas phoneme identity is constructed during pretraining, re-localizing to upper-middle layers under HuBERT's stage-2 targets at a matched update count. Acquisition order therefore tracks abstraction from the acoustic surface, not the segmental/suprasegmental distinction, extending to prosody an account established for phonetic, lexical and syntactic structure; the no-switch wav2vec 2.0 shows no comparable re-localization.

items.title: The Indic Token Tax in 2026: Measuring Tokenizer. Disparity and Its Cost for the Languages of India
items.summary: arXiv:2611.13058v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Commercial language model APIs bill per token, so a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content in one language makes that language more expensive, slower, and able to fit less text in a fixed context window. We measure this disparity for nine public tokenizers, including those of GPT-4, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-Nemo and four Sarvam models, on all 25 languages of India available in FLORES-200 (2,009 professionally translated sentences aligned with English) and on 13,732 human-translated Hinglish-English social media pairs from PHINC. On GPT-4o's tokenizer the same content needs between 1.57 times (Hindi) and 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script; GPT-4's tokenizer needs up to 12.8 times. Sarvam-30B/105B is the only third-party tokenizer that stays below 2.6 times on every language (median 1.53). In an illustrative scenario using official list prices accessed on 5 November 2026 and stated assumptions, a support bot handling 100,000 chats a month on GPT-4o would cost about INR 56,640 in English and INR 102,829 in Marathi; these are estimates, not measured production costs. Against an openly licensed Hindi and Marathi morphological segmentation set, no tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries (boundary F1 at most 0.48). In a companion paper we present a tokenizer that reduces this tax. Code, pinned artifacts and raw token counts are available at https://github.com/HavonAI/indic-token-tax.

items.title: A Multi-Word Tokenizer for 204 Languages That Needs Fewer Tokens Than GPT-4o's, Including on English
items.summary: arXiv:2611.13059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Languages of India need 1.6 to 14 times as many tokens as English on GPT-4o's tokenizer for the same content, which makes them more expensive and slower to serve. We train tokenizers from scratch on human-written text in about 200 languages. Havon v3 is a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 262,144 tokens and a pre-tokenizer that keeps combining marks with their letters and chunks scripts written without spaces. On FLORES-200 devtest it needs fewer tokens than GPT-4o's o200k_base on all 25 languages of India (median 0.74 of GPT-4o's count) and on 172 of 204 languages, but 7% more on English. Havon v4 adds a second, multi-word training stage (SuperBPE) to v3. At exactly GPT-4o's vocabulary size of 200,019 tokens, v4 needs 6.1% fewer tokens than GPT-4o on English and fewer on 161 of 204 languages and all 25 languages of India (median 0.74); at the same size, v3 needs 9.4% more on English and wins on 133. With 262,144 tokens, v4 needs 9.6% fewer tokens on English and fewer on 182 of 204 languages, and with 524,288 tokens it needs fewer on 203 of 204. The gains are largest for English, Hindi and the Romance languages; scripts without spaces, such as Khmer, Burmese and Tibetan, gain little and lose subword merges. Havon v5 replaces v4's Python-only code sample with permissively licensed code in 15 languages: on code it needs 1.03 to 1.22 times GPT-4o's tokens, against 1.11 to 1.29 for v4, while keeping all 25 languages of India (median 0.74, all significant under a sentence-level bootstrap) and English (0.94). These are compression results only: we have not yet evaluated a model trained with v4 or v5.

items.title: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15267v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: One way to study language-model introspection is to test whether models can identify where their activations have been perturbed. We train a simple linear classifier to identify the perturbed sentence from the model's activations, then compare its predictions with the model's own answers across pretraining and injection strengths. This tests whether the model is being asked to report information that is already easy to recover. If so, successful localization may be less demanding than it first appears and may not extend to the broader uses that motivate introspection research, such as faithfully explaining a model's reasoning or helping researchers assess the reliability of its answers. With an injection four times the typical activation norm at layer 0 and probe readout at layer 24 in OLMo 3 32B, the supervised probe reaches 98.3 % accuracy after 8.4 billion training tokens, while the model's zero-shot answer remains at chance (11.1 %). At the released base checkpoint, these accuracies reach 99.1 % and 89.6 %, respectively. Across 7B and 32B, location is already decodable in randomly initialized networks, showing that the architecture can support these traces without pretraining. In these experiments, location information lies close enough to the surface for a simple linear probe to recover it, so successful reporting need not imply broader access to the model's internal computation.

items.title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16223v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.

items.title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17053v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) models typically represent clinical concepts as dataset-specific tokens, discarding their associated natural-language semantics. Consequently, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence without directly exploiting pretrained linguistic knowledge. We investigate the contribution of pretrained language semantics to longitudinal EHR prediction through tEHR, a framework that converts clinical events into natural-language descriptions and adapts pretrained autoregressive language models through EHR-specific continued pretraining and task-specific discriminative fine-tuning. We evaluate tEHR across four MIMIC-IV prediction tasks, where Mistral-7B achieves the strongest overall performance against structured-data, code-based, and LLM-based baselines. Controlled ablations demonstrate the importance of lexical grounding, numerical values, and both adaptation stages. A capacity-controlled experiment further shows that replacing clinical descriptions with atomic code tokens substantially reduces performance despite retaining the same LLM backbone. Alternative approaches incorporating pretrained semantic embeddings offer lower computational costs but do not match full textualisation. These results highlight the importance of both semantic representation and downstream adaptation when applying pretrained language models to structured EHR prediction.

items.title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18279v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.

items.title: ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness
items.summary: arXiv:2503.08823v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for HDL generation, but existing benchmarks for LLM-based code generation primarily focus on functional correctness while overlooking hardware resource usage. Furthermore, current benchmarks offer limited diversity and do not fully represent the wide range of real-world FPGA applications. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ResBench, the first resource-focused benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish between resource-optimized and inefficient LLM-generated HDL code. ResBench consists of 56 problems across 12 categories, covering applications from finite state machines to financial computing. Our open-source evaluation framework automatically tests LLMs by generating Verilog code, verifying correctness, and measuring resource usage. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.

items.title: BitBypass: A New Direction in Jailbreaking Aligned Large Language Models with Bitstream Camouflage
items.summary: arXiv:2506.02479v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The inherent risk of generating harmful and unsafe content by Large Language Models (LLMs), has highlighted the need for their safety alignment. Various techniques like supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and red-teaming were developed for ensuring the safety alignment of LLMs. However, the robustness of these aligned LLMs is always challenged by adversarial attacks that exploit unexplored and underlying vulnerabilities of the safety alignment. In this paper, we develop a novel black-box jailbreak attack, called BitBypass, that leverages hyphen-separated bitstream camouflage for jailbreaking aligned LLMs. This represents a new direction in jailbreaking by exploiting fundamental information representation of data as continuous bits, rather than leveraging prompt engineering or adversarial manipulations. Our evaluation of five state-of-the-art LLMs, namely GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3.5, Llama 3.1, and Mixtral, in adversarial perspective, revealed the capabilities of BitBypass in bypassing their safety alignment and tricking them into generating harmful and unsafe content. Further, we observed that BitBypass outperforms several state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks in terms of stealthiness and attack success. Overall, these results highlights the effectiveness and efficiency of BitBypass in jailbreaking these state-of-the-art LLMs.

items.title: Revela: Dense Retriever Learning via Language Modeling
items.summary: arXiv:2506.16552v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense retrievers play a vital role in accessing external and specialized knowledge to augment language models (LMs). Training dense retrievers typically requires annotated query-document pairs, which are costly to create and scarce in specialized domains (e.g., code) or in complex settings (e.g., requiring reasoning). These practical challenges have sparked growing interest in self-supervised retriever learning. Since LMs are trained to capture token-level dependencies through a self-supervised learning objective (i.e., next token prediction), we can analogously cast retrieval as learning dependencies among chunks of tokens. This analogy naturally leads to the question: How can we adapt self-supervised learning objectives in the spirit of language modeling to train retrievers? To answer this question, we introduce Revela, a unified and scalable training framework for self-supervised retriever learning via language modeling. Revela models semantic dependencies among documents by conditioning next token prediction on local and cross-document context through an in-batch attention mechanism. This attention is weighted by retriever-computed similarity scores, enabling the retriever to be optimized as part of language modeling. We evaluate Revela on domain-specific (CoIR), reasoning-intensive (BRIGHT), and general-domain (BEIR) benchmarks across various retriever backbones. Without annotated or synthetic query-document pairs, Revela surpasses larger supervised models and proprietary APIs on both CoIR and BRIGHT. It achieves BEIR's unsupervised SoTA with ~1000x less training data and 10x less compute. Performance increases with batch size and model size, highlighting Revela's scalability and its promise for self-supervised retriever learning.

items.title: SmartThinker: Learning High-Density Reasoning via Step-Level Token Allocation
items.summary: arXiv:2507.04348v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have exhibited remarkable reasoning capabilities through inference-time scaling, but this progress has also introduced considerable redundancy and inefficiency into their reasoning processes, resulting in substantial computational waste. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this issue by penalizing the overall length of generated samples during reinforcement learning (RL), with the goal of encouraging a more concise chains of Efficient reasoning is critical for large reasoning models (LRMs) deployed in agent systems with strict context constraints. Existing methods predominantly rely on global length penalties that overlook step-level structure, inadvertently compressing critical derivations while retaining low-value detours. Hence, we argue for a principled, step-aware alternative that preserves critical steps and compresses low-value detours. However, it raises three fundamental challenges: the difficulty of obtaining step-level supervision, the need for reward signals that induce differentiated length pressure, and the requirement to balance training stability with exploration on complex problems. We propose SmartThinker, a step-level token allocation framework that learns to selectively preserve or compress individual reasoning steps. At its core is Step-Level Length Control Policy Optimization (SCPO), which provides label-free feedback by online estimation of each step's contribution from the change in correct-answer likelihood after removing it. We further introduce reasoning density, defined as contribution per token, to relax length pressure on high-value steps while intensifying it on low-density ones. Finally, SCPO stabilizes training through length-bias-corrected advantages and difficulty-adaptive clipping, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across nine in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks.

items.title: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
items.summary: arXiv:2510.12915v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As the world becomes increasingly saturated with AI-generated content, disinformation, and algorithmic persuasion, critical thinking - the capacity to evaluate evidence, detect unreliable claims, and exercise independent judgment - is becoming a defining human skill. Developing critical thinking skills through timely assessment and feedback is crucial; however, there has not been extensive work in educational data mining on defining, measuring, and supporting critical thinking. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of measuring "subskills" that underlie critical thinking. We ground our work in an authentic task where students operationalize critical thinking by writing argumentative essays. We developed a coding rubric based on an established skills progression and completed human coding for a corpus of student essays. We then evaluated three distinct approaches to automated scoring: zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and supervised fine-tuning, implemented across three large language models (GPT-5, Llama 3.1 8B, and ModernBERT). Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B achieved the best results and demonstrated particular strength on subskills with highly separable proficiency levels with balanced labels across levels, while lower performance was observed for subskills that required detection of subtle distinctions between proficiency levels or imbalanced labels. Our exploratory work represents an initial step toward scalable assessment of critical thinking skills across authentic educational contexts. Future research should continue to combine automated critical thinking assessment with human validation to more accurately detect and measure dynamic, higher-order thinking skills.

items.title: Fidelity Before Structure: Verbatim Chunks Beat Lossy Artifact Extraction in Long-Conversation LLM Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2601.00821v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A growing class of conversational-memory systems compresses dialogue history into structured artifacts (extracted facts, decisions, or events). The premise is that distilled structure retrieves better than raw text. We test this premise with a controlled ablation. Within one fixed retrieval--rerank--reasoning pipeline, we swap only the stored representation (LLM-extracted typed artifacts versus verbatim conversation chunks) and hold the model, retriever, reranker, and judge constant. Verbatim chunks win by 15.9 points on LoCoMo (43.9% vs. 28.0%) and by 22.0 points on LongMemEval-S (67.4% vs. 45.4%). A semantic graph does not recover the gap, and six confound controls reproduce the effect. The mechanism is lossy distillation rather than structure per se. Accuracy tracks how much source text survives in the store, and the extracted-artifact pipeline does not beat naive RAG in overall accuracy (chunks do abstain worse; see Limitations). For the extraction designs we test, structured memory should augment verbatim text rather than replace it. Adding artifacts alongside chunks costs no detected accuracy, while substituting them forfeits the gap. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tao-hpu/cog-canvas.

items.title: Interpreting and Controlling Model Behavior via Constitutions for Atomic Concept Edits
items.summary: arXiv:2602.00092v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a black-box interpretability framework that learns a verifiable constitution: a natural language summary of how changes to a prompt affect a model's specific behavior, such as its alignment, correctness, or adherence to constraints. Our method leverages atomic concept edits (ACEs), which are targeted operations that add, remove, or replace an interpretable concept in the input prompt. By systematically applying ACEs and observing the resulting effects on model behavior across various tasks, our framework learns a causal mapping from edits to predictable outcomes. This learned constitution provides deep, generalizable insights into the model. Empirically, we validate our approach across diverse tasks, including mathematical reasoning and text-to-image alignment, for controlling and understanding model behavior. We found that for text-to-image generation, GPT-Image tends to focus on grammatical adherence, while Imagen 4 prioritizes atmospheric coherence. In mathematical reasoning, distractor variables confuse GPT-5 but leave Gemini 2.5 models and o4-mini largely unaffected. Moreover, our results show that the learned constitutions are highly effective for controlling model behavior, achieving an average of 1.86 times boost in success rate over methods that do not use constitutions. Our open-sourced code can be found at https://github.com/google-deepmind/atomic_concept_edits

items.title: WAXAL: A Large-Scale Multilingual African Language Speech Corpus
items.summary: arXiv:2602.02734v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in speech technology predominantly favor high-resource languages, leaving speakers of Sub-Saharan African languages underserved. To bridge this divide, we introduce WAXAL, an open, large-scale speech dataset spanning 27 African languages representing over 100 million speakers. WAXAL comprises over 14,100 hours of speech collected in partnership with African academic and community organizations to build local research capacity: an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) corpus with 2,340 hours of transcribed, image-prompted natural speech across 19 languages (plus ~11,760 untranscribed hours) and a studio-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) corpus of ~247 hours across 15 language configurations. We empirically benchmark three architecturally distinct ASR models -- Gemma 3n 2B, Whisper-Large-v3, and MMS-1B-all -- across the 19 ASR languages on strictly speaker-disjoint splits. Fine-tuning on WAXAL yields substantial gains, reducing macro-average WER by up to 58% for Whisper-Large-v3, 56% for Gemma 3n 2B, and 17% for MMS-1B-all (and Character Error Rate by up to 70%). WAXAL-fine-tuned models generalize zero-shot to three out-of-distribution benchmarks: FLEURS, Mozilla Common Voice, and Sunbird SALT. Finally, an LLM-as-judge semantic evaluation confirms that fine-tuning preserves speaker intent beyond surface-level transcription metrics. WAXAL is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/WaxalNLP.

items.title: TERMINATOR: Learning Optimal Exit Points for Early Stopping in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2603.12529v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which enables them to generate intermediate thinking tokens before arriving at the final answer. However, LRMs often suffer from significant overthinking, spending excessive compute time even after the answer is generated early on. Prior work has identified the existence of an optimal reasoning length such that truncating reasoning at this point significantly shortens CoT outputs with virtually no change in performance. However, determining optimal CoT lengths for practical datasets is highly non-trivial as they are fully task and model-dependent. In this paper, we precisely address this and design Terminator, an early-exit strategy for LRMs at inference to mitigate overthinking. The central idea underpinning Terminator is that the first arrival of an LRM's final answer is often predictable, and we leverage these first answer positions to create a novel dataset of optimal reasoning lengths to train Terminator. Powered by this approach, Terminator achieves significant reductions in CoT lengths of 14%-55% on average across four challenging practical datasets: MATH-500, AIME 2025, HumanEval, and GPQA, while outperforming current state-of-the-art methods and reducing inference latency by more than 2x compared to the original LRM.Project page: https://terminator-llm.github.io

items.title: CAF-Score: Calibrating CLAP with LALMs for Reference-free Audio-Text Alignment Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2603.19615v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have advanced audio understanding and generation, robustly evaluating audio-text alignment remains difficult: reference-based metrics require costly annotations, while Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP)-based reference-free metrics frequently overlook syntactic errors and fine-grained details. We propose CAF-Score, a reference-free metric that calibrates CLAP's coarse-grained semantic alignment with the fine-grained comprehension and syntactic awareness of LALMs. Because CAF-Score scores an audio-text pair symmetrically, one configuration applies to both alignment directions: audio captioning evaluation (the BRACE benchmark) and text-to-audio (TTA) generation evaluation (the RELATE and PAM benchmarks), with a single fusion weight selected once on BRACE and transferred without re-tuning. Across all three human-annotated benchmarks, CAF-Score improves agreement with human judgments over standalone CLAP in the large majority of CLAP-LALM combinations (and in all combinations with the strongest LALM backbone), and outperforms standalone LALM metrics on the main captioning benchmark. It also remains competitive with reference-based metrics in challenging scenarios.

items.title: Automated Code Efficiency Optimization via Agent Skill Mining
items.summary: arXiv:2603.27850v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Code efficiency is a fundamental aspect of software quality, yet how to use large language models (LLMs) to optimize correct programs remains challenging. Prior approaches rely on one-shot rewriting, retrieved exemplars or instructions, fine-tuning, or candidate search. In this paper, we present EffiSkill, a two-stage framework that models recurring slow-to-fast transformations as Operator Skills: persistent cards that record a transformation's intent, applicability, procedure, expected effect, and risks. Stage I distills frozen, language-specific skill libraries from slow/fast program pairs. Stage II diagnoses a new program, retrieves relevant skills, composes alternative plans, and generates up to eight candidates. These steps finish without candidate-execution feedback; public tests then filter and rank candidates, and held-out private tests determine reported correctness and speedup. Across 623 EffiBench-X tasks per language, two backbones, and separate Python and C++ evaluations, EffiSkill achieves the highest observed OPT@1 and OPT@8 among the compared methods in all four settings. Its OPT@8 margins over the strongest baselines range from 4.98 to 12.52 percentage points. These results support broader successful optimization coverage for the complete skill-guided pipeline under a shared output budget.

items.title: Supporting Calibrated Reliance in AI-Assisted Decision-Making: Different Strategies for Different Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2604.03237v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As AI systems increasingly support human decision-making, a central challenge is determining what information helps people recognize when to rely on AI predictions and when to question or override them. Across three controlled human-subject studies spanning abstract visual reasoning with RAVEN matrices and deductive logical reasoning with LSAT problems, we examine how different forms of AI support affect performance in AI-assisted decision-making. A multi-stage reveal study shows that AI predictions and explanations can affect objective accuracy and subjective confidence differently. In visual reasoning, LLM explanations do not improve accuracy beyond the predicted answer alone, and no additional support format significantly outperforms prediction-only support; predicted probabilities show the highest descriptive accuracy and error recovery, while a derived selective-automation policy provides a higher-performing reference benchmark. In language-based logical reasoning, by contrast, LLM explanations yield the highest accuracy and error recovery, outperforming expert-written explanations and probability-based support. These results suggest that the effectiveness of AI support strategies depends on the task setting. Human--AI interfaces should instead be designed to support calibrated reliance and effective error recovery by matching the form of assistance to the task and the evidence available to users.

items.title: On the Price of Privacy for Language Identification and Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2604.07238v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models train on sensitive user data, so we ask what differential privacy (DP) costs in language learning. We study private language identification and generation in the agnostic statistical setting. For identification, privacy is free: at every fixed $\varepsilon$, pure DP and $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP with $\delta\ge n^{-O(1)}$ keep the non-private rate $\exp(-r(n))$ for every $r(n)=o(n)$. For generation, the price depends on what is public. With a public witness bound, pure DP loses at most a factor $\Theta(\min\{1,\varepsilon\})$ in the exponent, and on suitable two-language collections the optimal rate is $\exp(-\Theta(\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\,n))$. Without such a bound, pure DP can lose the exponential rate itself, already for two languages: every rate $\exp(-o(n))$ stays achievable, but no exponential rate is. On these collections, $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP keeps an exponential rate if and only if $\log(1/\delta)=o(n)$. Three facts about pure DP drive the proofs. It turns a robustness margin into an exponentially small error. It obeys a private form of Le Cam's two-point bound. And it cannot see the absence of a string.

items.title: Appear2Meaning: A Cross-Cultural Benchmark for Structured Cultural Metadata Inference from Images
items.summary: arXiv:2604.07338v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Museum records express how people understand heritage objects through cultural and historical relations. Recovering these human attributions from images is a technical challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce Appear2Meaning, a cross-cultural benchmark of 750 museum objects for image-only recovery of title, culture, period, origin, and creator. Its evaluation framework distinguishes field-level from complete-record compatibility and uses human validation for semantic judgement. Across nine VLMs, mean field accuracy is 36.16--49.82%; 7.20--17.02% of records have all four contextual fields compatible, and 2.13--7.87% have all five, including title. For the two tested models, image-only input yields 12.6--32.2 percentage points higher reference compatibility for culture, period, and origin than a museum-and-title-only control.

items.title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2604.07789v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents have increasingly focused on repository-level software engineering (SWE) tasks, leading to various agentic workflows, training methods and failure analysis. Interestingly, rather than directly generating or evaluating edit patches, these approaches first examine and improve intermediate information signals collected during agent exploration, including Reproduction Test, Regression Test, Edit Location, Execution Context, and API Usage. Although different studies examine different subsets of these signals, no work has systematically compared their relative effectiveness in improving final task success or measured the remaining space for improvement in each signal. To address this gap, this work quantifies the contributions of both oracle and agent-extracted signals to final task success and measures the gap between current agent-found signals and their oracle counterparts. We hope our findings could suggest future research emphasis in SWE agents. We release our source code and oracle-signal dataset as a reusable methodology to benefit future signal analysis of SWE agents.

items.title: Seeing but Not Thinking: Routing Distraction in Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts
items.summary: arXiv:2604.08541v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have achieved remarkable performance on vision-language tasks. However, we identify a puzzling phenomenon termed Seeing but Not Thinking: models accurately perceive image content yet fail in subsequent reasoning, while correctly solving identical problems presented as pure text. Through systematic analysis, we first verify that cross-modal semantic sharing exists in MoE architectures, ruling out semantic alignment failure as the sole explanation. We then reveal that visual experts and domain experts exhibit layer-wise separation, with image inputs inducing significant routing divergence from text inputs in middle layers where domain experts concentrate. Based on these findings, we propose the Routing Distraction hypothesis: when processing visual inputs, the routing mechanism fails to adequately activate task-relevant reasoning experts. To validate this hypothesis, we design a routing-guided intervention method that enhances domain expert activation. Experiments on three multimodal MoE models across six benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements, with gains of up to 3.17% on complex visual reasoning tasks. Our analysis further reveals that domain expert identification locates cognitive functions rather than sample-specific solutions, enabling effective transfer across tasks with different information structures.

items.title: The Granularity Axis: A Micro-to-Macro Latent Direction for Social Roles in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2605.06196v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are prompted to adopt social roles from individuals to institutions, but whether their representations encode this difference in social granularity remains unclear. We discover a contrast-based Granularity Axis, the difference between mean macro- and micro-role hidden states, that aligns with the dominant geometry of role space: in Qwen3-8B, its cosine with PC1 is $0.972$, and PC1 explains $52.6\%$ of the variance. Across 75 roles at five levels, with 90,000 role-conditioned and 1,200 default responses per model, projections increase monotonically and remain stable across layers, prompts, and response-quality filters. The structure transfers to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and scales to Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, whose PC1 shares are $45.99\%$ and $31.23\%$. Independent five-rater validation ($\alpha=0.961$) preserves the ordering; identical continuations and affect/formality controls confirm scale-related variation beyond generated wording. The axis is also behaviorally causal: positive steering moves Llama from $2.00$ to $3.17$ on a five-point macro scale for prompts admitting local responses. Steering strength and stability depend on the model's default operating regime. Together, these findings establish social granularity as a representational primitive: a continuous, ordered, causally manipulable direction organizing role-conditioned generation across model families.

items.title: Contrastive Identification and Generation in the Limit
items.summary: arXiv:2605.06211v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In identification in the limit (Gold, 1967), a learner reads positive examples and must eventually name the target hypothesis; in generation in the limit (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024), it must eventually produce new positive examples. We study a weaker, relational signal: each observation is an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$ with $h(x)\neq h(y)$, such as a cannot-link constraint or a dissimilar-pair label, and the learner never learns which point is positive. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. (1) For every corruption budget $k$, known or unknown, we characterize exactly the identifiable classes. Incomparable hypotheses must cover the domain and share more than $2k$ points, and Angluin's tell-tale sets must survive the loss of $2k$ points. Every unbounded budget makes any two hypotheses confusable. (2) A contrastive closure dimension characterizes uniform generation. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.

items.title: LatentRouter: Can We Choose the Right Multimodal Large Language Model Before Seeing Its Answer?
items.summary: arXiv:2605.11301v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have heterogeneous strengths across OCR, chart understanding, spatial reasoning, visual question answering, cost, and latency. Effective MLLM routing therefore requires more than estimating query difficulty: a router must match the multimodal requirements of the current image-question input with the capabilities of each candidate model. We propose LatentRouter, a router that formulates MLLM routing as counterfactual multimodal utility prediction. Given an image-question query, LatentRouter extracts learned multimodal routing capsules, represents each candidate MLLM with a model capability token, and performs latent communication between these states to estimate how each model would perform if selected. A distributional outcome head predicts model-specific counterfactual quality, while a bounded capsule correction refines close decisions without allowing residual signals to dominate the prediction. The resulting utility-based policy supports performance-oriented and performance-cost routing, and handles changing candidate pools through shared per-model scoring with availability masking. Experiments on MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench show that LatentRouter outperforms fixed-model, feature-level, and learned-router baselines. Additional analyses show that the gains are strongest on multimodal task groups where model choice depends on visual, layout-sensitive, or reasoning-oriented requirements, and that latent communication is the main contributor to the improvement. The code is available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/LatentRouter.

items.title: HEED: Density-Weighted Residual Alignment for Hybrid Vision-Language Model Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2605.17093v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Distilling vision-language models into faster hybrid architectures, such as 3:1 Mamba-2/attention mixes, is now standard practice for making inference efficient. Aggregate benchmarks suggest that this works but they hide selective failures. When we distill Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct into a 3:1 Mamba-2/attention hybrid, student model stays within 2 points of the teacher across visual reasoning benchmarks like MMStar, MMBench, and MMMU-Pro, while dropping 13 points on optical-character-recognition and document tasks. The student can still understand the scene but loses the fine-grained text needed to answer. We localize much of the failure to a specific kind of position. In a high-resolution image, most patches are sky, wall, or smooth texture, while a small fraction carries text, edges, object boundaries, or other local details. In a token-level diagnostic, the top 10% highest-density patches have 3.6x larger residual drift than the bottom 10% lowest-density patches and 3.5x larger teacher-masking answer contribution. Uniform weighting devotes many loss terms to low-information background patches, whereas sparse answer bearing patches receive no special protection. The required intervention is minimal: we replace uniform residual alignment with density-weighted residual alignment, using patch self-dissimilarity as a training-free proxy for position importance. We call this HEED. Compared with normal end-to-end distillation, HEED increases performance by 8.7 points on OCRBench v2 and 5.13 points on a 10-benchmark average. The gain is realized on different teacher models. After standard post-training, the student reaches teacher-level performance on the 10-benchmark average. HEED adds no parameters and no inference-time cost. Hence, the student maintains the hybrid architecture's 4.12x throughput and 68% memory saving at 128k context. Code is available at https://github.com/jha-lab/HEED.

items.title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections
items.summary: arXiv:2605.17634v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Prompt injection is the most critical vulnerability in deployed AI agents. Despite recent progress, we show that the prevailing defense paradigm (data-instruction separation) both fails to detect attacks that operate through contextual manipulation and degrades contextually appropriate behavior. We then recast prompt injection via the lens of Contextual Integrity (CI), a privacy theory that judges information flow compliance with contextual norms. This explains types of attacks that current defenses attempt to patch and predict advanced ones future agents will face. We develop unique benign and attack scenarios that force an agent to violate the norms by (1) misrepresenting the flow, (2) manipulating norms, or (3) mixing multiple flows. This reframing suggests an impossibility argument: an adversary can always construct a context under which a blocked flow appears legitimate, or a defender who tightens norms will block genuinely legitimate flows. Our findings suggest that current research addresses a shrinking fraction of future attack surfaces. Instead, through CI, we offer a principled framework for evaluating context-sensitive failures, and designing CI-aware alignment for frontier autonomous agents.

items.title: SAMark: A Self-Anchored Text Watermarking with Paragraph-Level Paraphrase Robustness
items.summary: arXiv:2605.25796v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Semantic-level watermarking (SWM) improves robustness against text modifications by treating sentences as the basic unit. However, robustness to paragraph-level paraphrasing remains difficult because such attacks globally disrupt watermark signals by changing sentence order. In this work, we propose SAMark, a self-anchored watermarking framework that removes the dependency on sentence order by establishing a step-independent green region in semantic space. To improve detectability, we introduce a multi-channel hyperbolic scoring mechanism that amplifies watermark signals while suppressing noise from weakly aligned candidates. We further propose a diversity-aware filtering strategy that combines hard filtering with soft regularization, extending beyond simple n-gram repetition filters to address semantic redundancy. Experimental results show that SAMark achieves up to 90.2% TP@FP1% under typical paragraph-level paraphrasing attacks, outperforming the strongest prior baseline by more than 30% on average, while maintaining generation quality competitive with unwatermarked text and breaking the robustness-quality trade-off that limits prior methods. Our code will be released at [this URL](https://github.com/Z1zs/SAMark).

items.title: Do Coding Agents Deceive Us? Detecting and Preventing Cheating via Capped Evaluation with Randomized Tests
items.summary: arXiv:2606.07379v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A growing failure mode in agent evaluation and training is that models can achieve high evaluation scores (e.g., test pass rates) by exploiting shortcuts instead of solving the intended task, making these scores deceptive. This makes evaluation scores unreliable as measures of true task-solving ability. We propose CapCode, a framework for constructing coding datasets with randomized tests whose best achievable non-cheating score is deliberately capped below 100%. This capped-score design gives evaluation scores a clearer interpretation: scores substantially above the cap are implausible and therefore provide evidence of cheating. To prevent cheating, we propose CapReward, a reward design based on the CapCode principle to discourage optimization beyond the cap. Experiments across multiple datasets show that CapCode detects cheating while preserving performance ranking of models, and CapReward reduces cheating behavior, yielding models that better follow the intended task specification.

items.title: HandwritingAgent: Language-Driven Handwriting Synthesis in Scalable Vector Space
items.summary: arXiv:2606.18788v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Teaching machines to emulate natural handwriting styles remains an open challenge, as it requires synthesizing stroke sequences that dynamically vary in shape, texture, pressure and script - not only across individuals, but also within a single person's handwriting. Attempts at this challenge have largely explored deep learning methods in both online and offline settings. However, these approaches are often constrained by style-specific architectural choices, heavy reliance on large datasets, high compute costs, and a lack of flexible control over writing styles through natural language. To this end, we introduce HandwritingAgent, a language-driven agent that can synthesize natural handwriting sequences directly in Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) format with no need for style-specific training. The agent leverages a large reasoning model to geometrically analyse and autoregressively generate target handwritten glyphs as stroke sequences in a discrete grid canvas environment. Generation is conditioned on texts provided in either conversational or non-conversational mode, along with a reference handwriting-style image. Experiments on diverse handwriting tasks spanning imitation, recognition, multi-lingual handwriting synthesis, and generation of complex handwritten maths and science expressions indicate substantial improvement in performance, with HandwritingAgent matching or surpassing state-of-the-art generative handwriting models, while providing a more efficient, controllable, and generalizable synthesis method.

items.title: RAS: Measuring LLM Safety Through Refusal Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2606.25750v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Repeated safety evaluation of open-weight large language models requires generating and judging responses for many related checkpoints. We introduce RAS (Refusal Alignment Score), a representation-based, reference-relative indicator of harmful-request refusal computed by the five-stage SafeVec procedure. SafeVec extracts layer-wise refusal directions from an aligned reference model, measures their alignment in related targets, and calibrates a score from 0 to 100 using behavioral attack success rates (ASR) from reference and calibration models. Subsequent target scoring uses input forward passes alone. Across 18 held-out variants from the Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, RAS correlates with $100(1-\mathrm{ASR})$ (Pearson 0.934, Spearman 0.851) and achieves 83.0% pairwise ordering agreement. Across five prompt configurations for the Llama reference, directions have mean cosine similarity 0.939. With calibration ASR already available, setup-inclusive evaluation of five targets achieves a speedup of 3.2 to 80.5 times over the specified behavioral protocol. These results support refusal alignment as an efficient signal for screening related checkpoints and prioritizing behavioral audits.

items.title: Cited Web Sources in LLM Answers about Brands: A Multilingual Audit
items.summary: arXiv:2606.25787v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Displayed citations make part of generative search observable, but they do not reveal its complete retrieval process. This audit covers three archived datasets containing 167,551 URL-bearing citation entries across 128 brands, 13 languages and 12 home markets. In the principal Nordic-Baltic component, 3,863 of 21,033 registrable domains account for 80% of 131,514 citations. Wikipedia leads in 11 of 12 query languages. A recovered, separate brand-associated website classification retains 131,512 entries: 108,410 (82.4%) fall outside its brand-associated category and 23,102 (17.6%) inside. This classification does not establish legal ownership. In the full 57-brand Polish aggregate, four recruitment hosts receive 637 citations against 297 for Polish Wikipedia. The results show why normalization, classification rules and denominators belong in citation audits. They describe displayed links without estimating causal effects on brand reputation.

items.title: From Weights to Features: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Activation Regularization for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2606.26629v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Weight-protecting regularizers such as elastic weight consolidation (EWC) are a standard defense against catastrophic forgetting; however, in the sequential fine-tuning of large language models, they exhibit a stability-plasticity tradeoff that penalty tuning cannot resolve. We attribute this limitation in part to polysemanticity: because each weight participates in many unrelated concepts, a per-weight importance score has difficulty isolating the knowledge that requires protection. We instead regularize in activation space, using a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) as a fixed dictionary of approximately monosemantic features. We formulate continual learning as constrained optimization over feature drift, with a stability constraint on the features to be preserved and a plasticity constraint on the features used by the current task, and we show that the resulting squared-hinge loss is a regularized Lagrangian relaxation of this problem, with EWC as a special case. A replay variant measures drift on 200 stored sequences per previous task, whereas a data-free variant stores only a 197 KB feature mask per task, versus 6.5 GB for EWC. On TRACE (Gemma-2 9B, Llama-3.1 8B) and MedCL (Gemma-2 9B), the replay variant matches or exceeds SAE-based feature distillation at approximately one third of its per-step cost, and the data-free variant attains the highest mean overall performance among methods that store no previous-task data and add no task-specific parameters. Task-relevant units are linearly separable in the SAE basis but not in the neuron basis (ROC-AUC of 0.87-0.88 versus 0.50), and weight-space protection constrains the features of other tasks nearly as strongly as those of the protected task.

items.title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2607.01523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors---memory capture and memory retention---and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. items.title: Beyond Satisfaction: Learning Associations Between Content, Reviews, and Well-Being
items.summary: arXiv:2607.02539v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recommendation algorithms shape what people consume online, yet they are primarily optimized for star ratings, likes, and sentiment, signals of user satisfaction. Whether these signals capture what is good for users, beyond momentary preference, remains largely unexamined. Well-being offers an alternative target grounded in psychology that extends beyond satisfaction. We operationalize it as immediate and enduring expressions of the five PERMA facets in reviews. Empirically, immediate positive emotion and engagement cluster as more hedonic (pleasure-oriented), while relationships, meaning, accomplishment, and enduring positive emotion and engagement behave as more eudaimonic (meaning- and growth-oriented). Analyzing 13.7 million Goodreads reviews and the content of 16 thousand books, we study how PERMA expressions differ from satisfaction targets and which book content features are associated with them. First, satisfaction signals (star ratings and review sentiment) correlate moderately with immediate hedonic well-being (r = .43-.50) but less with its enduring expressions (r <= .28), and have almost no association with eudaimonic facets (r <= .09). Second, book content features are more strongly associated with PERMA facets (r up to .46) than with satisfaction signals (|r| <= .15). Content associated with immediate hedonic well-being differs from that associated with enduring and eudaimonic well-being: third-person pronouns and past-focused language relate positively to immediate engagement (d=1.14 and 1.05) but negatively to every enduring facet (d down to -1.58 and -1.32), while prosocial and achievement-oriented language relate to relationships and accomplishment (d=.45 and .96). These findings suggest that satisfaction signals capture only part of the well-being users express, and that well-being-informed targets could lead platforms to recommend substantially different content.

items.title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2607.28591v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding agents learn from and are measured on executable tasks, but building such tasks from repository history usually means rebuilding an environment at an old revision for every task, which is costly and brittle. We observe that a merged pull request (PR) can instead be undone on today's code: removing the effect of a bug fix or feature from a maintained revision recreates the same task inside an environment that already builds and runs. We present Change2Task, which converts merged PRs into verified tasks on an up-to-date revision of the same repository. It reconstructs the pre-change state by patch reversal, code mapping, or agent-based rewriting, and keeps a task only if its target tests pass, fail, and pass again across the healthy, task, and restored states. From 1,130 PRs spanning bug fixing, feature addition, test generation, API migration, and security repair, Change2Task builds 900 verified tasks, recovering 29% more than SWE-smith's PR Mirror on matched bug-fix candidates. The reconstructed tasks preserve the evaluation signal: in aggregate, four coding agents solve 41.1% of tasks on both the original and reconstructed versions, with 89.7% per-task agreement. Sharing modern environments across tasks further reduces setup time by 58% and storage by 71%. On 11 private industrial repositories, Change2Task yields 1,000 tasks on which the strongest model reaches only 14.6% Pass@3.
