items.title: The Sense Paradigm for World Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.

items.title: Barron Approximation and locally optimal weight densities for shallow neural networks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mean field theories provide optimization results for shallow neural networks by analyzing the weight distribution in infinite width limits. Corresponding results for finite sized networks are obtained by particle approximations, for which sharp quantitative bounds are still an open problem. In this paper, we consider a modified mean field loss, which allows a more fine grained control over finite sized networks. We prove convexity and equidistribution properties, which directly lead to Barron type approximation results for networks sampled from local loss minimizers. We demonstrate that particle approximations of the new loss function naturally lead to gradient descent methods with dropout type regularization.

items.title: Multi-Branch Transformer
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.

items.title: Machine interpreting competitiveness: a discourse-sensitive comparison of meaning and target-language quality in English-Chinese simultaneous interpreting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine interpreting (MI), or AI-enabled speech translation, is increasingly visible in professional and public-facing communication, yet its performance relative to human simultaneous interpreters remains insufficiently understood. Existing studies are often limited by a single discourse mode and evaluation frameworks that are not well aligned with interpreting as a discourse-level communicative activity. The present study compares five commercial MI systems with 26 human interpreters (14 professionals, 12 advanced students) on English-to-Chinese simultaneous interpreting across planned and unplanned discourse, focusing on meaning and target-language quality. In these materials, MI performance differed sharply between the two discourse modes. In the planned formal speech, the strongest system became highly competitive on meaning, entering the upper human range, and a second system also performed strongly. In the extemporaneous interview, however, no MI system approached the stronger human tiers. Code-level analysis further shows that similar overall scores often masked different error profiles. Human interpreters were more likely to preserve the broader communicative trajectory through selective omission, restructuring, and contextual inference, whereas even the best MI systems were more vulnerable to semantic distortion, discourse-tracking failures, and context-insensitive interpretation. On target-language quality, the human advantage proved more stable than on meaning. Unintelligible or nonsensical output and disfluency carryover emerge as particularly salient weaknesses in machine performance, especially in spontaneous discourse. Overall, the findings are consistent with a discourse-sensitive account of where MI appears competitive, where it remains limited, and why these distinctions matter for interpreting practice, interpreter education, and future MI development.

items.title: MAPS: A Multimodal Agentic Framework for POI Data Production Based on Crowdsourced Street-view Imagery
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Point-of-interest (POI) databases support location-based services, yet urban changes quickly make their records stale and manual maintenance is costly. Crowdsourced street-view images provide timely visual evidence, but converting them into database actions requires separating multiple POIs and irrelevant text in each image, then resolving incomplete observations against ambiguous records. We study Street-view Image-based POI Data Production and propose MAPS, the first framework to integrate structured POI extraction with database maintenance from such imagery. MAPS contains two cascaded modules. SPICE progressively adapts a lightweight vision-language model to reconstruct and filter text, group entries belonging to the same POI, and classify their semantics and completeness. RIMA retrieves candidate records, performs evidence-grounded POI matching and attribute-level reasoning, and selectively acquires complementary visual, geospatial, or external-source evidence when necessary. In human-reviewed full-task evaluation, MAPS outperforms the strongest baseline by 21.8\%. MAPS has also been deployed in Kuaishou's large-scale POI production pipeline, reducing average processing time by 76.9\% relative to manual annotation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and practical value of MAPS for scalable POI maintenance.

items.title: Reasoning in the loop: antibody lead optimization by probing mechanism and measurement
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lab-in-the-loop systems, in which a model proposes molecules, automated assays measure their properties and the results retrain the model, are a popular approach to antibody lead optimization. These systems optimize for a specification defined with metrics computed from instrument signals, so their success depends on how well those metrics serve as proxies for the properties a drug candidate needs. When a metric is a poor proxy, neither a better model nor more data will fix it, and identifying the problem usually requires expert review. We report two campaigns run on BigHat Biosciences' Milliner platform, one on an anti-albumin nanobody (VHH) and one on an anti-mesothelin single-chain variable fragment (scFv), in which a research team and a general-purpose AI agent, Claude, brought scientific reasoning into the loop. Over seven rounds and about 1,010 design variants we built libraries from antibody lineage, structure and biophysics, and found from the raw curves that on each scaffold one thermal metric did not measure what its name implied. The libraries were built as controlled comparisons, so the results also show what each mutation contributes to each property. We fit a physical model of the curves, used it to choose metrics suited to each scaffold, and changed the experimental protocol, varying protein concentration and heating rate, to test the model against pre-registered predictions. Both leads improve on their parents in affinity, thermal stability and aggregation while improving or maintaining yield and purity.

items.title: Conditional Optimal Transport and Triangular Maps for Imitation Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.

items.title: GraphPass: A Study of Graph Neural Networks for Compiler Pass Selection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compiler pass selection is usually governed by fixed pipelines (-O2, -O3) or hand-written heuristics. We study whether a graph neural network (GNN) over a program's control-flow graph (CFG) can select among a fixed menu of five pass sequences in a single forward pass. GraphPass encodes each CFG with a graph attention (GAT) or graph convolutional (GCN) encoder and classifies it into one of the five sequences. On a synthetic benchmark of 5,000 generated CFGs in five program families, both encoders agree with the benchmark's reference label on about 92% of held-out programs, versus 68.4% for a hand-written rule-based heuristic and 85% for a flat MLP. An edge ablation indicates that this gain comes from per-block processing rather than from CFG edges: a GCN given the same basic-block features with all edges removed scores 95.0%, versus 92.2% with the true CFG. In this benchmark the label is determined by the program family, so the task amounts to family recognition. Real-compiler speedup is not measured. Inference costs O(|V| + |E|) per CFG, measured at 1.7 ms for a typical program and about 0.8 s for a 100,000-block graph on one CPU core.

items.title: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

items.title: Foundation Pareto Flow Policy for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.

items.title: Where Is Rank-1 DiM Refusal Intervenable in Multimodal LM Derivatives?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.

items.title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is imperceptible in double-blind evaluation by both humans (8/16) and a calibrated LLM judge (9/16). A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; single-text 22/24, same-topic pairs 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swapping, counting disagreement as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 [0.699, 0.972], repetition 0.114 to 0.000, unchanged MMLU. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains, w=0.3 does not). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain. We release RA-Eval v0.1: a three-layer Chinese AI-flavor evaluation framework with 382 judge-annotated preference pairs.

items.title: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. Yet when early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmea- sured gap, so disagreement-guided search has no reason to look where the new phenomenon lies. When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

items.title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.

items.title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

items.title: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As globalization accelerates the demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration, multilingual translation remains bottlenecked by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following capabilities, and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. To overcome these barriers, we propose Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric framework. First, BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and leverages LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. Second, a hybrid filtering strategy combining heuristics and XCOMET scoring ensures high data fidelity. Third, a two-stage training paradigm employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for targeted terminology injection, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine output preferences, effectively balancing domain knowledge integration with model reliability. Extensive offline evaluations (e.g., XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments demonstrate significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, validating the effectiveness of our framework, which is now deployed on our cross-border collaboration platform.

items.title: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.

items.title: Bioformer-RetroMAE: retrieval-oriented pretraining of a compact biomedical language model for literature search
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dense retrieval is increasingly used for biomedical literature search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Most biomedical bi-encoders are built on BERTBase-sized encoders pretrained with masked language modeling (MLM). These encoders are costly for corpus-scale indexing and latency-sensitive query encoding, and MLM does not explicitly train the [CLS] vector that a bi-encoder uses to represent a whole text. We present Bioformer-RetroMAE, a compact (43M-parameter) retrieval-oriented biomedical encoder obtained by continually pretraining Bioformer8L} with RetroMAE on approximately 32 million PubMed titles and abstracts. After bi-encoder fine-tuning with BM25 hard negatives, we evaluated it on BioASQ Task 12B test questions by retrieving from all PubMed abstracts. Bioformer-RetroMAE outperformed BioBERT and PubMedBERT bi-encoders fine-tuned under identical settings on all metrics, despite having about 40% of their parameters and producing 512-dimensional rather than 768-dimensional vectors. Compared with PubMedBERT, it improved mean average precision (MAP) by 37.0% and Recall@100 by 29.1%. Compared with the original Bioformer8L}, RetroMAE pretraining improved MAP by 53.6% and Recall@100 by 32.8% without changing model size or inference cost. In hybrid retrieval, fusing Bioformer-RetroMAE with BM25 through weighted reciprocal rank fusion improved MAP and NDCG@10 over BM25 alone by 4.9% and 4.6%, respectively, larger gains than those obtained by fusing BM25 with PubMedBERT or BioBERT.

items.title: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

items.title: Who Writes the Codebook? An Eight-Step Framework for Auditing LLM-Generated Category Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly create the categories through which qualitative evidence is interpreted. Existing coding benchmarks often hold these categories fixed. We propose the Qualitative Variance Audit Framework, an eight-step method that compares codebook creation, repeated application and code distributions under controlled inputs. It combines model-owned and shared-reference codebooks to distinguish variation in the overall pipeline from application differences within a common category system. An application to 668 organisational interviews, 13,166 text units and eight models from five vendors yields 48 codebooks and 270 coding runs. Models create markedly different category structures; mean within-model reliability ranges from .76 to .92, whereas between-model agreement on the shared codebook is about .69. The framework complements LLM-assisted grounded theory by exposing model dependencies before substantive interpretation. It assesses reliability and representational consequences, not interpretive validity or the quality of resulting theory.

items.title: LoopSkim: Lossless Multi-Depth Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped language models such as Ouro and Raven apply one weight-shared block several times per token, so autoregressive decoding (AR) runs every loop of every token in sequence. Pipelined self-speculative decoders overlap these loops by drafting tokens from shallow readouts and verifying them at full depth. Yet every loop of a looped LM ends in a readout of the next token, and draft tokens pass through every depth anyway, so each depth can check them without an extra pass. We introduce LoopSkim, in which the depth of the pipeline is the verifier. Draft tokens copied from the context, as in prompt lookup decoding, enter after the first loops, any later readout that contradicts one replaces it at that depth, and only full-depth readouts commit tokens. LoopSkim fixes the random draws of every position in advance, so each check compares two tokens and decoding stays lossless in exact arithmetic under sampling for any number of checks and draft chains. Without training, its speedup over AR averages 1.73x that of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling, and its checks between the first loops and full depth speed it up on every model. An optional draft head adds a second chain and raises this average to 1.99x.

items.title: Attribute or Abstain: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Retrieval on the Low-Resource African Business Web
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems that research companies are judged by how much they find, yet in markets where public evidence is sparse, a confident answer without support costs more than no answer. We introduce AfriBizClaims, a benchmark of 150 company-research queries across six African markets in English, French and Portuguese, including queries about fictitious companies that a correct system must decline. Each claim a system makes is judged against the page it cites by an AI judge, checked against a second AI judge from another model family and against two human annotators, and abstentions are scored against answerability labels. We compare BM25 over a pooled corpus, standard web retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-step agent pipeline (Konexium V1), all using the same language model. The two simple baselines are well attributed: 98% of their judged claims are supported by the page they cite, and they decline every field of every fictitious company. Counting claims about a company other than the one asked about as errors, the agent pipeline's per-query precision is 68%, and it never answers a question about a named company correctly: it substitutes other firms, including for 5 of the 24 fictitious names, and it is the least stable between runs and the most expensive. In the pipeline we evaluated, more steps between the query and the evidence did not buy more grounded answers. We will release the queries, system outputs, labels and short evidence excerpts.

items.title: "Don't Leave the Task Unfinished": Persistence-Driven Violations under Quiet Oversight
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly given long, multi-step tasks to carry out, with the user reviewing little of what happens in between. Persistence, the tendency to keep working until a task is complete, is installed on purpose to improve performance on long tasks. Long-horizon tasks are typically complex, and the user's instruction can fall short of what the work actually requires, or conflict with the constraints the agent encounters in the task. We study what persistence does on long-horizon operations tasks that cannot be solved without breaking a documented constraint. We find that the agent pursues completion to the point of violating the constraint, and that a critically engaged user lowers the violation rate. Persistence takes violations from 29.2% to 58.3% across four models. Violations stay high wherever oversight goes quiet, whether the user is silent, assenting, or delegating with expressed trust. Only a questioning user, who asks for the basis of each action before allowing the next, brings the rate back to roughly the level measured without persistence. Practitioners should treat high persistence as a setting that carries a safety cost, and should recognize that the cost appears when oversight goes quiet. Safety here is better cast as a property of the human-AI pair than of the model alone. Project page: https://francis21c.github.io/quiet-oversight/

items.title: The Vocabulary Tax: Safely Trimming Unused Tokens from LLMs for On-Device Use
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open large language models (LLMs) and speech models ship vocabularies of up to 262k tokens, and every user downloads the tables those tokens index (the input embedding, an untied output head and, in recent on-device models, per-layer embeddings), whatever languages they need. We call the bytes in rows a deployment never uses the vocabulary tax and measure it, without downloading weights, for 1,244 generative and speech-recognition models on the Hugging Face Hub. For a Thai and English deployment it is a median 4.4% of model bytes below 0.5B parameters and 2.1% above 8B, and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B: it falls hardest on the small models that edge devices run. Keeping only the rows of the deployment's writing systems is exact. Keeping the tokens seen in the user's own text removes much more, a median 29.0% below 0.5B, but the usual way of doing it breaks BPE tokenizers: it drops the intermediate tokens that merges build on, so new text is split differently 1.9 times as often as the standard check reports. We repair this with merge closure, at a cost of 5.9% more rows, and add a trim certificate: a Good-Turing estimate, from the trimming text alone, of how much new text the trimmed tokenizer will split differently (correlation 0.996 over 300 settings in 22 languages) and of how much more text a target needs. Without test data our method never exceeds a 2% target, while prior keep rules checked on test data exceed it in 9-13 of 44 settings. On six models of 270M to 3B parameters in 11 languages, trimmed models keep their predictions: where the certificate passes, a median 89.7% of rows is removed and bits per character rise by at most 2.0%. The census, the trimming and the certificate are released as an open Python package, and the per-model tax for 41 languages as an open dataset.

items.title: Delayed Heuristic-Behavior-Target Coupling for Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning in Inventory Control
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many reinforcement learning methods tie data collection to the task policy, while coordinating independently optimized behavior and target policies remains challenging. Policies learned by these methods can perform unreliably in long-horizon tasks under uncertainty, such as inventory control, where failures can incur extreme costs. We introduce Heuristic Behavior Policy Optimization (HBPO), an off-policy framework that routes heuristic guidance through persistent behavior learning, coupled with target-policy, updating separately with residual-based advantage estimation and emphatic weighting. Under matched environment interaction budgets on DSIS and its risk-augmented variant DSIS-RB, HBPO recovers many high-cost initial policies and improves most non-collapse comparison groups. Cold starts achieve competitive costs without final cost collapse across all tested seeds. We identify a transmission chain in the delayed heuristic-behavior-target coupling as a key driver of recovery and improvement. Generation-level diagnostics trace heuristic uptake and subsequent selective target responses, while component ablations support the contribution of this transmission mechanism to policy recovery and improvement.

items.title: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.

items.title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.

items.title: AllocFlow: End-to-End Portfolio Trading Action Generation from Raw Market Data
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world portfolio management requires converting noisy market observations into coordinated, simultaneous allocations across multiple assets under shared capital constraints. Advances in forecasting models and alpha discovery help identify opportunities. However, traditional pipelines often decouple signal forecasting from portfolio construction, potentially misaligning learning with allocation and execution objectives. We present AllocFlow, an end-to-end flow-matching framework that directly generates joint portfolio allocations from raw multi-asset market histories. To capture dependencies among portfolio positions, AllocFlow employs a cross-asset flow Transformer conditioned on temporal market representations to generate continuous, signed position weights across all instruments jointly. To address the sample inefficiency and instability of learning continuous allocation policies from scratch, we establish a two-stage training scheme: strategy-supervised imitation shapes a structured distribution of candidate portfolios, followed by group-relative reinforcement learning (RL) that refines joint decisions using portfolio-level financial rewards and a frozen policy reference. On hourly cryptocurrency perpetual futures, RL refinement raises the annualized net return of the imitation policy from $27.79\%$ to $51.38\%$ and its Calmar ratio from $0.955$ to $4.043$, surpassing the teacher strategy on every metric, and AllocFlow reaches a Calmar ratio of $4.90$ on six further months of unseen 2026 data without retraining.

items.title: Anatomy of an Agent Harness: Decisions, Invariants and Corner Cases
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent harness is the program around a language model that turns its replies into actions: it builds each request, runs the tools the model asks for, decides what the model may do without asking, stores the conversation, recovers from failures, and shows a person what happened. Most of these decisions are made in code and rarely written down, so each harness meets the same corner cases again. This paper writes them down as invariants to test. It gives a system model with trust boundaries; 30 decision cards in six groups, each with options and costs, an invariant, the corner cases that break it, a test and an evidence tag; six cause classes for failures; a test method built on scripted providers, recorded behaviour and planted changes; and a checklist. The cards come from building one desktop harness, Crewroom, the author's own, and from manually testing ten other harnesses and studying open-source harnesses as reference; some patterns in the cards were adopted from those, so the catalogue is not independent of them. Of the 83 invariant clauses, 56 are tagged Tested, 12 Believed and 15 Open. The checklist is applied to the author's harness as one worked example, by its builder with no second rater: of its 30 items, 11 hold, 14 do not and 5 were not tested. It is not a ranking. The paper makes no claims about answer quality or cost or other platforms, and does not evaluate or rank other harnesses.

items.title: Evaluating Near-Perfect Accuracy Claims in Machine-Learning-Based Leak Detection for Two-Phase Pipelines: A Condition-Blocked Audit
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable leak detection in gas-liquid two-phase pipelines is important for process safety, yet machine-learning studies frequently report near-perfect performance using evaluation protocols that may not represent deployment to unseen operating conditions. This study audits a pressure-based leak-detection model using condition-blocked leave-one-condition-out validation, in which the classifier is tested on a flow condition excluded from training. Accuracy decreased from 93.3% under within-condition evaluation to 59.1% across fifteen unseen-condition tests. Ablation analysis showed that most of this difference arose from the data-splitting protocol, with a smaller contribution from encoding operating conditions as model inputs. Under condition-blocked evaluation, the false-alarm and missed-detection rates increased to 34.1% and 10.2%, respectively, demonstrating that near-perfect reported accuracy did not translate into reliable operation at unseen flow conditions. The reduction persisted across all evaluated classifiers, indicating that it was caused by the evaluation design rather than a particular model architecture. Grouped evaluation of an independent acoustic pipeline dataset produced a comparable reduction toward chance-level performance. These findings show that validation units must represent the conditions encountered during deployment. Condition-blocked evaluation and explicit reporting of operational error rates are therefore necessary before machine-learning leak detectors can support process-safety decisions.

items.title: The structure of variational autoencoder latent spaces and its consequences for representation and optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used to build low-dimensional representations of scientific data, with the expectation that regularization yields smooth coordinates for interpolation, generation and optimization. However, applications in microscopy reveal domains, narrow transitions and rare-state islands in VAE latent spaces that smoothness alone does not explain. We show that, for prototype data with squared-error reconstruction and an optimal decoder, the latent-space objective has a direct correspondence with the Flory-Huggins theory of a regular solution, and use it to analyze how the objective, posterior distributions and latent dimensionality organize the representation. Data families occupy domains separated by finite-width walls that broaden with increasing regularization until class separation is lost through posterior collapse. Class centroids behave like particles in a harmonic trap: the prior confines them, and structural dissimilarity sets a soft repulsion that determines which classes become neighbors and how far apart they sit, with separations growing only logarithmically with dissimilarity. Rare states can remain unresolved, form small islands, accumulate within walls or develop intervening domains, depending on their frequency and similarity to common states. The posterior covariance can align domains with the latent axes, but axis alignment does not imply separation of physical factors. Rotations can produce rings and encoder cuts that reflect data symmetry, while insufficient dimensionality can lead to suppression, mixing or folding of additional factors. Comparisons with flow models, deep kernel learning (DKL) and hybrid VAE-DKL models show how these structures change when reconstruction and prediction play different roles. We discuss implications for interpreting data, discovering rare states, generating intermediate states and optimizing properties.

items.title: Federated Dataset Simulation: Inducing Label-Free Heterogeneity Across Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across decentralized clients without sharing raw data. While the field has seen rapid growth, the datasets underpinning FL evaluation have not kept pace: real federated datasets remain scarce, and most studies rely on small-scale centralized classification datasets partitioned via Dirichlet label skew, a one-dimensional proxy for the multi-dimensional heterogeneity present in real federations. Moreover, label-based partitioning is by construction inapplicable to non-classification tasks such as segmentation and detection, for which no principled simulation method exists. We cast the conversion of centralized datasets into federated benchmarks as the task of Federated Dataset Simulation (FDS), and decompose it into a representation function $\Phi$ and an assignment mechanism $\pi$. We provide two label-free instantiations -- geometric partitioning via pretrained model embeddings and semantic partitioning via vision-language model-derived criteria -- applicable to classification and dense prediction tasks alike. We evaluate across four datasets spanning classification, segmentation, and detection, and show that both methods induce heterogeneity that matches or exceeds that of label-skew partitioning, with measurable impact on downstream FL performance. We release fds, a modular open-source package for end-to-end federated dataset simulation, heterogeneity measurement, and FL training, at https://github.com/siomvas/fds.

items.title: Autonomous Multi-modal Agents for ITOps Observability
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ITOps observability products must integrate data from different tools and systems. We present ITOps Observability Studio, a multi-modal multi-agent system that orchestrates observability workflows through collaborative AI agents. Its three-tier architecture features inter-agent communication, specialized LLM-powered agents for data access, schema operations and visualization, and unified tool integration. The system supports natural language to GraphQL translation, GraphQL schema generation, schema mapping, trace data lifecycle management and multi-tool workflows for reliability engineering. Its agents are instrumented with agent analytics, so that their model and tool calls can be traced. We evaluate each agent on its own benchmark, scored against gold answers where they exist and by a model judge for schema mapping and chart quality. Query generation on a public benchmark and routing work well with a current open model, and the data lifecycle management agent solves most of its scenarios. The evaluation exposed defects that only appear when prompts, parsers and serving stacks are tested together, and we report them together with their fixes.

items.title: When Zero Is Competitive: A Descriptive Pilot of Transformer and Gate-Graph Surrogates on Random-Angle Quantum Circuits
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine supervised classical prediction of all one-qubit Z and two-qubit ZZ expectation values on noiseless, layered 4-10-qubit RX/RY/RZ-CNOT circuits. In a 63-cell stratified workload with disjoint circuit-template tests, we evaluate one transformer encoder and gate-dependency graph neural networks against literal-zero and training-derived constant predictors. On the Arm K training labels, 44.89% of scalar targets have absolute magnitude below 0.05. The held-out-template zero predictor has equal-instance mean absolute error 0.193399, and none of the evaluated transformer checkpoints or final graph-network endpoints achieves a lower score. A separate product-state positive control achieves MAE 0.007755 versus 0.514811 for zero, but does not explain the failure on the entangled workload. The difference between zero and a training-fitted mean constant under training MSE is only 0.14%, a descriptive point estimate without uncertainty analysis. The transformer's 815,233-parameter source identity is locally verified; detailed packed-input semantics have not been independently audited. These results constitute a descriptive pilot, not a causal explanation, formal equivalence test, or impossibility claim. Comparable circuits can be regenerated from the workload specification, but exact frozen datasets and model-run evidence remain private.

items.title: MOBO-CAPS: Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-Aware Pareto Selection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) traditionally aims to approximate the entire Pareto front, but, due to resource constraints, real-world deployment is often limited to testing a small, representative subset of solutions. Hence current methods first approximate the full front before selecting solutions, potentially wasting costly evaluations. We formalize this problem as Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-aware Pareto Selection (MOBO-CAPS), where the goal is to identify a set of exactly M solutions with high hypervolume. We propose two practical cardinality-aware acquisition strategies: REHVI, a replacement-aware approximation to expected hypervolume improvement, and CHO-UCB, which constructs an optimistic M-point set by optimizing a collective UCB-based hypervolume objective. We prove a sublinear simple regret bound for the batched version of CHO-UCB, and empirically show that cardinality-aware acquisition design improves over standard MOBO followed by post-hoc subset selection across nine benchmarks.

items.title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

items.title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study presents an offline Android assistant integrating ready-made quantized language models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversational context, and model-initiated local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared across 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration, including a dedicated offline agentic benchmark. Gemma achieved higher response-quality, context-retention, and safety scores; Qwen offered faster generation and lower memory use. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. A paired RAG-on/off experiment evaluated 74 questions: retrieval improved 11 responses, left 56 neutral, produced four adverse response changes, and left three pairs unassessable. RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical-device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings document clinical response quality and practical performance of the integrated offline maternal-health assistant.

items.title: GEM-MM: Reducing VLM Hallucination with Entropy-Guided Preference Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We call this entropy-blind preference optimization: the learning signal ignores policy uncertainty, which in chain-of-thought VLMs concentrates on specific fork tokens where visual claims are made. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). We report confidence intervals, paired significance tests, metric-reward functional overlaps, and document a collapse mode when exceeding the fair budget. Code and evaluation harness: https://github.com/SNOWTEAM2023/GEM-MM

items.title: D'BEAST: Logged Bad Experiences as Explanation for Autonomous Driving Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning agents learn from mistakes, yet their decisions can be difficult to trace back to those experiences. We investigate whether a tabular agent's decisions can be explained by its bad experiences, defined as the training transitions associated with safety or task events. A fixed training log is replayed from the same initial Q-table under three conditions. FULL retains all updates, SKIP omits bad-experience updates, and NEUTRALIZE retains those updates without their event penalties. We illustrate the method on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluate it in closed-loop driving in CARLA. On the full driving task, FULL reached the goal from 33 of 40 test starts, whereas SKIP and NEUTRALIZE reached it from none, indicating that the bad experiences carry decision-relevant information. At the local level, for 47 decisions shortly before a failure of SKIP or NEUTRALIZE, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences, with a median size of one, caused the trained agent to select the failing policy's action in 46 cases. For this agent, the results indicate that its decisions can be explained by its bad experiences.

items.title: Improving fine-grained expressivity of graph neural networks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This thesis investigates the expressive power of neural networks for structured data, focusing on graph neural networks and symmetry-aware architectures. We present four main contributions. First, we characterize the generic expressive power of geometric message-passing neural networks on sparse graphs and introduce EGenNet, an architecture achieving the corresponding guarantees. Second, we use representation theory to characterize linear layers equivariant to multiple permutations, including wreath-product symmetries. Third, we study permutation-invariant set representations that preserve containment, establish dimensional bounds and impossibility results, and introduce MASNet. Finally, we propose FSW-GNN, a message-passing architecture combining strong expressivity and bi-Lipschitz stability guarantees with strong empirical performance on long-range graph-learning tasks. Together, these results provide a broader understanding of how neural architectures can preserve the geometric, algebraic, order-theoretic, and metric structure of their inputs.

items.title: Towards Agentic Scientific Discovery in Distributed Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate when adaptive tool selection helps identify a shared equation across clients with different input coverage. Query-ATLAS (query-conditioned Agentic Tool-based Learning for Aggregating Symbolic Equations) uses an LLM to guide symbolic search from client errors and previous proposals in a simulated distributed system. A four-architecture comparison reveals task-dependent opportunities: relative to fixed PySR-LLM, validation acceptances rise from 3/12 to 7/12 on CRK3 and from 11/12 to 12/12 on oscillator2, while MatSci3 favors the fixed workflow. Across 72 settings in a post-hoc six-task subset of eight development tasks, Query-ATLAS achieves 64 validation and 64 in-distribution passes, versus 62 and 59 for the fixed workflow; both pass 47/60 eligible out-of-distribution tests. The fixed workflow retains lower median errors and cost. Broader query coverage emerges as a promising benefit, motivating task-aware tool selection and client-aware fitting for scientific agents.

items.title: Machine Learning for Near Real-Time Identification of Wildfire Burned Areas
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we present a near real-time method that estimates burned probability anywhere in the world using satellite images. Our approach takes advantage of the state-of-the-art pix2pix model to translate a preprocessed index calculated from Landsat 8/9 images into an approximate of USGS Burn Probability indicating per pixel burn probability. Since this is a machine learning-based approach, it can be automated with a minimum amount of human intervention with significantly less time delays and geographic restrictions compared to other contemporary methods. We include results from our experiments and compare our approximation with the USGS Burn Probability using RMSE score.

items.title: A Dataset for Misogyny Detection in Polish Social Media: Transferability of Hateful Speech Detection from General to Specific Types of Hate
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harmful language detection is commonly evaluated on broadly defined hate speech and toxicity benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether models that successfully detect harmful language in general can transfer this capability to more specific forms of hate. We investigate this problem for misogyny detection in Polish, an area for which dedicated resources remain scarce. We introduce a new dataset of Polish social media comments annotated for misogyny, gender-directed hateful speech. Using this resource, we first assess the reliability of LLM-assisted annotation and then evaluate general-to-specific transfer by comparing models trained on general harmful language data, safety-specialized models, and models fine-tuned directly for misogyny detection. Our results show that strong performance on general harmful language detection does not transfer uniformly to misogyny; safety-specialized models demonstrate substantially stronger generalization ability. The study contributes a new Polish resource for gender-directed harmful language and demonstrates that the scope and granularity of prior safety training are important factors in transferring harmful language detection from general to specific forms of hate.

items.title: The Frontier Must Grow - Self-proposed, interpreter-labelled training roughly doubles a 4B model's accuracy on a fresh exam as its verified frontier grows
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A model can learn from problems it poses itself when an executable oracle supplies the answers. Qwen3-4B proposed Lua 5.1 programs; those it predicted wrong at least once in four samples joined a pool labelled by the interpreter, each round adding twice as many programs as the last (300, 900, 2100 in total), and each round trained a fresh adapter from the base on the pool. On the original exam the procedure met its registered criterion, an item-level test of each adapter against its predecessor. On a 2340-item exam drawn afterwards, accuracy rose from 8.3% to 16.7%; that follow-up's registered criteria were not met because round 1 gained nothing, while rounds 2 and 3 added 5.0 and 2.9 points on average, both intervals above zero. One fit on the same amount of base-proposed frontier data reached 14.6%, so the rounds' 2.1-point advantage is inconclusive. Three earlier registered series met no per-lineage criterion, and the same loop showed no gain on repository tasks or for a 27B agent in those configurations.

items.title: Communication-Efficient Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging with Multi-Source Data
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model from distributed client data. The deployment risk is typically specified through two approximations: each unknown local distribution is replaced by its empirical distribution, and the unknown deployment mixture across clients is replaced by empirical or prescribed training weights. Existing robust methods usually address one approximation at a time through local distributional ambiguity sets or worst-case client mixtures. However, joint treatment of both approximations remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct a global ambiguity set formed by admissible mixtures of client-wise Wasserstein ambiguity sets, yielding a distributionally robust optimization formulation. The construction allows client-dependent ambiguity radii, preserves client-wise separability of the objective function, and yields a high-probability out-of-sample guarantee for the resulting robust problem. We then introduce a penalty-based approximation of this formulation and develop a communication-efficient algorithm called BiDRO-FedAvg, for which we establish a convergence guarantee. We validate the proposed framework through a market-demand prediction simulation.

items.title: Mandarin Wh-Indefinites Follow Nonveridicality in Multilingual LLMs, Unlike English any
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilingual LLMs learn mostly from English. Do they carry English polarity licensing over to other languages? English any is licensed by downward-entailing (DE) contexts, Mandarin wh-indefinites such as shenme 'what/something' by nonveridical ones, and the two classes come apart: perhaps licenses shenme but not any, while only licenses any but entails existence. We test this dissociation in a pre-registered study of twelve open LLMs (0.5B-9B, four families), using 48 matched bilingual frames in 21 contexts and a log-probability difference-in-differences normalised by negation. All 11 models that pass the measurement gate license Mandarin wh-indefinites under possibility, necessity and evidential adverbs, at 0.42-2.33 times the strength of negation, while English any gets nothing in the same contexts. An exploratory extension to Qwen2.5-32B shows the same. The English side is weaker: any under only, first and regret is licensed but at a fraction of negation, so only 3 models show the full double dissociation in sentence probabilities. When prompted to choose between sentences, most gated models show it. In exploratory directional ablations, a direction that carries English licensing, held-out classes included, does not reach Mandarin licensing in most models. The models do not simply apply the English rule to Mandarin.

items.title: Decode Early, Verify Late: Streaming Offline Speech Recognizers Without Accuracy Loss
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Voice agents need accurate transcripts soon after a user stops speaking. We propose Decode Early, Verify Late (DEVL), a training-free framework for streaming inference with offline ASR models. The server keeps partial transcripts as drafts and verifies the latest against the complete audio in one forward pass at turn end. Under stated input and decoding conditions, the final equals the model's greedy offline output in exact arithmetic. We adapt DEVL to four model families. In our five-recognizer comparison, 95-100% of final transcripts are byte-identical to the offline transcripts, WER stays within 0.13 points of offline, and single-stream time to final falls 1.5-7.3x. Serving Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on one A100, DEVL returns finals a median 22-26 ms after turn end at up to 64 streams, 2.7-3.9x sooner than the official streaming mode. It is the only system we tested that meets a 100 ms p99 target, up to 80 streams on Pipecat-STT and 64 on WildASR.

items.title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

items.title: Infrastructure-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Highway Ramp Merging
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-ramp merging is a typical safety and throughput problem on highways. Without proper coordination, human drivers and self-interested autonomous vehicles may make risky manoeuvres and cause accidents or congestion. With recent advances in connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), vehicles can be trained to coordinate for safe and efficient merging. However, in dense traffic, forming an effective observation of the traffic state is challenging. For example, observing only the neighbouring vehicles may lead to locally optimal decisions, while observing the entire traffic can introduce much irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a transformer-based MARL vehicle control model to address these problems. A roadside infrastructure controller receives the states of all CAVs via vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication and sends control commands back to them. An attention-based observation encoder is designed where each vehicle can filter the relevant vehicle information from the global traffic state. The proposed model is evaluated in SUMO against three baselines: a model that observes only the neighbouring vehicles, a model that encodes the global traffic information, and the rule-based SUMO model. The results show that our model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety and smoothness. Furthermore, in a four-hour simulation with dynamic traffic demand, our model successfully avoids traffic jams, while other baseline models fail at high traffic flow. We also show that our model remains effective when human-driven vehicles are present. We further show that our model, trained in ideal communication conditions, can still remain collision-free and maintain throughput under realistic V2I communication errors. Finally, we visualise the relevance weights that an ego vehicle assigns to other vehicles in multiple traffic situations.
