items.title: Latent Annealed Posterior Sampling with a Variance-Preserving Local Gaussian Approximation for Sparsely Observed Random Fields
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20659v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Posterior inference for random fields from sparse observations presents two major challenges: accurately characterizing complex spatial uncertainty and controlling conditional sampling costs as spatial resolution increases. We propose latent annealed posterior sampling (LAPS). LAPS first maps the random field into a lower dimensional latent space, while a Branch--Trunk coordinate decoder enables field evaluation at arbitrary spatial locations. Flow matching then learns the latent prior distribution. Based on this learned prior, LAPS performs posterior sampling through multilevel annealing. At each level, prior flow transport generates a reference state, which is combined with Gaussian noise using variance-preserving coefficients to construct a local Gaussian approximation of the conditional prior. This approximation is then combined with the observation likelihood to define a local posterior, from which latent posterior samples are generated using preconditioned MALA. Numerical experiments show that LAPS accurately approximates posterior distributions, preserves distinct posterior modes, and decouples posterior conditioning from output resolution. Across two Gaussian benchmarks, LAPS closely matches exact posterior references, with sliced Wasserstein distances $1.8\%$ and $2.4\%$ higher than those obtained from independent exact posterior samples. In the bimodal posterior benchmark, LAPS reduces the sliced Wasserstein distance from $0.2693$ to $0.1499$ and consistently recovers both modes across all test scenarios. For the two dimensional Navier--Stokes random field, LAPS substantially improves marginal posterior calibration while maintaining nearly constant evaluation time as the output grid is refined from $64^2$ to $192^2$. These results demonstrate that LAPS offers a favorable tradeoff among posterior accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and computational efficiency.

items.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21390v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Collaborative edge large language model (LLM) systems often require repeated prefill computation when task contexts are transferred between agents. Reusing previously computed key--value (KV) caches can eliminate this overhead, but requires KV-cache delivery before the receiving agent begins decoding. Under strict deadlines and unreliable edge links, complete KV cache transfer may be infeasible, making the timely delivery of useful KV information critical. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that combines prioritized source transmission with adaptive loss recovery. PriorityFEC first organizes KV blocks into a utility-aware source queue to prioritize important information. It then employs ACK-sliding Streaming FEC and a lightweight Double Deep Q-Network (Double-DQN) scheduler to dynamically balance source delivery and repair transmission under deadline constraints. We implement PriorityFEC in a distributed edge LLM-serving prototype and evaluate it using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple workloads. Experimental results demonstrate that PriorityFEC preserves more useful KV information and achieves substantially higher task accuracy than competing transport schemes, particularly when the deadline is insufficient to deliver the complete KV cache.

items.title: When the Editing Intent Is Split: A Cross-Modal Jailbreak Attack for Large Image Editing Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23909v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large image editing models increasingly infer editing intent from both textual and visual inputs, creating an underexplored safety risk when harmful intent is distributed across modalities. In this work, we formalize this split-intent vulnerability and propose the Split-Intent Jailbreak Attack (SIJA), which asymmetrically distributes an unsafe editing intent by specifying the editing referent in text while concealing the safety-critical action and specification through graphical visual semantics in an auxiliary cue. To systematically study this threat, we introduce the Split-Intent Image Editing Safety Benchmark (SI2ESBench) for evaluating image editing models under split-intent inputs. Extensive experiments on representative commercial and open-source models demonstrate that SIJA effectively compromises state-of-the-art image editing systems, achieving ASRs of 68.28% on GPT Image 2 and 91.38% on Qwen-Image-3.0-Pro. Our results expose a mismatch between multimodal editing and safety assessment: the distributed intent can be recovered to execute the requested transformation, yet its harmfulness often remains undetected by existing safeguards. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose editing-intent reconstruction, a defense principle that explicitly evaluates the complete transformation implied by the joint multimodal context and substantially improves rejection of split-intent attacks. Our findings expose a cross-modal safety gap in modern image editing systems and highlight the need to assess the jointly inferred transformation rather than individual inputs in isolation. Project page: https://github.com/yexianmin/SIJA.

items.title: Who Plans, Who Edits? Verified, Cost-Aware Division of Labor for LLM-Driven Analog Layout Repair
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24234v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language-model agents can repair analog layouts when sign-off tools check every edit, but which model should plan a repair, which should edit it, and at what cost remain open questions. In our tool-grounded repair agent, models only choose bounded layout operators; sign-off tools rerun each task's contract checks after every edit, so failing layouts are never accepted. On layout-versus-schematic (LVS), design-rule checking (DRC), and post-layout repairs of three designs (a production high-voltage digital-to-analog converter (DAC), a 5-V oscillator, and a SKY130 operational transconductance amplifier (OTA)) with six tier-matched models from two vendors, 182 blind runs show that cheap models execute plans but rarely succeed alone (the cheapest model: 1 of 11 runs alone, 16 of 17 under a flagship planner; p < 0.001), cheap planners fail more often, and no fixed assignment is cheapest on every task. We propose a learning controller that selects models for each role and the escalation order from the first tool evaluation and updates Bayesian estimates after every attempt. With rules and initial estimates frozen before testing, the controller fixed 7 of 8 episodes on four sealed held-out tasks, matching the OpenAI flagship alone, at 15-40% of the flagship's spend per fix on three tasks but 8% higher spend overall. The cheapest mid-tier model alone fixed 6 of 8 at the lowest overall spend per fix but missed the hardest task. All 32 extracted DAC repairs match the human-guided LVS repair's integral nonlinearity (INL) within 0.005 least significant bits (LSB) at every code.

items.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28907v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

items.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37584v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We formalize item-level preference distillation on the SID prefix tree, deriving an exact factorization of item preference distributions into prefix conditionals and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into conditional KL terms. Guided by this decomposition, we renormalize the generator's probabilities over legal next tokens and match the resulting distributions to the teacher's conditional preferences along the ground-truth SID path, jointly optimizing the distillation objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation and demonstrate that REGER consistently outperforms existing GR baselines while retaining efficient inference.

items.title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as Control for AI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38214v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input-output examples. How many such specifications must users provide, and which ones, for the agent to implement a program that fulfills their intent? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, because it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure - that is, a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions - which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, users cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering such structure from thousands of lines of generated code. To address this issue, we introduce Skeleton Coding, a process in which humans jointly specify the structure in high-level, code-like format, alongside behavioral specifications for the desired outcome. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests users must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15-26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.

items.title: Combinatorial Residual Network: a decay-chain-aware classifier without explicit jet assignment
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40749v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Final states with several jets from the decays of heavy particles pose a combinatorial problem: the jets must be assigned, at least implicitly, to their parent particles. The Combinatorial Residual Network (CoReNet) is a classifier that encodes the assumed decay chain in its architecture, building the event representation level by level along the decay hierarchy and combining all jet assignment hypotheses, evaluated with shared weights, with learned weights. The exchange symmetries of the decay are built in, the network size does not depend on the number of hypotheses, and no generator-level jet assignments are used in training. Developed for the $b\bar{b}b\bar{b}$ final state and used in several CMS searches, CoReNet with 1508 parameters performs well above kinematic baselines on fast-simulated Higgs boson pair production against QCD multijet events and trains in minutes on a single GPU, and its hypothesis weights select the truth-matched jet pairing in most signal events in which it is defined. Since only the encoded decay chain is specific to the final state, we test the construction on $HH \to b\bar{b}W^+W^-$ against semileptonic $t\bar{t}$, where encoding the decay chain of the background as well improves the classification at a cost of about $10^{3}$ parameters. In both final states, CoReNet performs comparably to a state-of-the-art transformer-based network more than two orders of magnitude larger. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/cms-cmu/CoReNet.

items.title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41398v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. Its local message passing keeps computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. We further embed GraphMP in a beam-search algorithm that progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. To turn this decoding effort into lasting improvements, we propose the decoder model factory, a paradigm for training successive models on data collected by earlier models during decoding. In our implementation, verified search trajectories provide reusable training data for distilling knowledge into subsequent models. Across generations, the model factory yields a search-enhanced decoder that is broadly competitive with Relay-BP. On the largest code block, which encodes $4612$ logical qubits, it achieves a lower logical error rate and about $20$ times the decoding throughput of the standard Relay-BP baseline. These results motivate a coupled quantum-classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning adapts the models to changing noise conditions. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that continually produces high-performance, low-latency decoders for evolving quantum hardware.

items.title: Zero-shot evaluation of open vision-language models as System 1 decision models on radiology tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01631v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Purpose: To compare two multimodal System 1 decision models (Clef 27B, d1 3B) with three generative vision-language models read out zero-shot from a single answer token (Qwen3.8-27B, which is Clef's backbone; Gemma 4 31B; MedGemma 1.5 4B) on seven radiology tasks. Methods: All models ran locally on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The System 1 models returned a probability for each option in one pass; for the generative models, probabilities were read from the log-probabilities of the option letters. Tasks covered chest CT and radiograph reports (CT-RATE, PadChest), device MR safety records (GUDID), tubes and lines on chest radiographs (RANZCR CLiP), chest CT volumes (CT-RATE), brain MRI motion (MR-ART) and MRI sequence (BraTS 2021), 4,435 cases in total. The primary endpoint was AUROC with bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: All five models retrieved report findings well (AUROC 0.93-0.99). Clef ranked higher than its backbone on CT volumes (0.749 vs 0.668) and tube and line radiographs (0.812 vs 0.766) and lower on motion (0.625 vs 0.709), but it changed decisions more than ranking: it identified 90 of 100 FLAIR volumes, a class its backbone never chose, and cut calibration error on CT volumes from 0.436 to 0.072. d1 was within 0.04 of Clef on reports while using 3 to 9 times less energy per request, but was weak on images. Gemma 4 31B ranked device MR safety best (0.854) and MedGemma 1.5 4B ranked motion best (0.821), yet MedGemma was at chance on MRI sequences and answered "severe" for 93% of motion scans. Conclusion: A single-token readout turns open generative models from several families into usable decision models without retraining, but no model was best on every task and each had task-specific answer biases, so models and decision thresholds should be chosen on local cases.

items.title: IssueLighter: An Issue Type-Aware LLM Agent for Issue Report Validity Assessment
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02721v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Invalid issue reports are prevalent in open source software (OSS) projects, imposing substantial burdens on maintainers who already face a high risk of burnout. Prior research has primarily focused on identifying invalid reports for specific issue categories (e.g., bug and wontfix), leaving the broader landscape of OSS issue types largely unexplored and limiting the generalizability of existing approaches. Moreover, existing methods provide little support for explaining or validating their predictions, reducing their practical usefulness for maintainers. With the rise of LLM-based agents, it remains unclear whether a comprehensive understanding of the causes of invalidity across all issue types can improve validity assessment performance while producing well-grounded rationales. To this end, we first manually annotated the validity status of 520 issue reports from three OSS projects, i.e., pandas, scikit-learn, and mypy, resulting in 257 invalid reports and 263 valid ones. Then, we conducted a thematic analysis on these invalid reports and identified 13 causes of invalidity that are closely specific to issue types. Based on these insights, we propose IssueLighter, an agent-based framework with a type-aware validity assessment strategy that dynamically executes commands. Experimental results show that IssueLighter consistently and substantially outperforms all baseline methods, with an average F1 improvement of over 20 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm that both the type-aware strategy and the taxonomy of causes of invalidity contribute to the performance gains. Qualitative analysis further demonstrates that IssueLighter generates rationales grounded in accurately identified causes of invalidity and supported by evidence. Moreover, leveraging these rationales, we challenged maintainers' original decisions in four disputed cases, and all received approval.

items.title: Progressive Multi-Scale Super-Resolution via Cascaded Bicubic Anchors and Inter-Scale Mutual Refinement
items.summary: arXiv:2611.03390v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Super-resolution networks are trained for one magnification factor, so several output resolutions require several models. We propose PMS-SR, a progressive single-input multiple-output network that produces x2, x4, and x8 results in one forward pass, with a Transformer backbone on the low-resolution grid. In Stage 1, each scale is predicted as a residual over the detached bicubic upsampling of the previous scale's prediction. With Dirac and zero initialization, training starts exactly from the bicubic cascade, and each head adds only the band the previous scale lacks. In Stage 2, inter-scale mutual refinement couples the scales in both directions through space-to-depth feedback, deformable alignment, and per-pixel fusion, so x8 features refine the x2 output. Trained on DF2K, the 7.95M-parameter model achieves a higher PSNR than every compared multi-scale method at x4 and x8 on all five standard benchmarks. At x8, it outperforms the x8-specific DRN-L on all of them, leads all compared methods on Urban100, and is within 0.13 dB of the best result elsewhere. Against three single-scale SwinIR-M models, PMS-SR uses 22% of the parameters, runs 2.9x faster on BSD100 inputs, and its outputs agree 6.7-12.4 dB more closely. Code and pretrained models will be released at https://github.com/julian135707/PMS-SR upon acceptance.

items.title: Toward an Optimal Configuration for Tree Species Classification from Bark Images: A Leakage-Safe Ablation Study
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05680v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Identifying tree species from bark photographs matters for forest inventory and the wood-processing industry, yet the design choices behind deep-learning approaches have not been studied systematically, and some reported results may be inflated by images of the same trunk appearing in both training and test sets. We present a systematic ablation on BarkNet 1.0 (20 species) under a tree-level, leakage-safe five-fold cross-validation, using ConvNeXt-V2 backbones with attention-based multiple instance learning (AMIL). We vary patch size, aggregation strategy, training regime, backbone capacity, the whole-image baseline, and test-time bag size, and we measure leakage directly with a matched image-level split. Per-patch accuracy rises with patch size (75.2% at 160 px to 89.3% at 512 px), and image-level accuracy plateaus near 94.9% at 512 px. AMIL exceeds majority voting by at most 0.7 pp; soft voting and mean pooling do no better than hard voting, so the gain comes from the learned attention weights and vanishes at 512 px, where attention is near-uniform. Backbone capacity changes accuracy by less than a point, and two-stage training gives no advantage. Whole-image classification (91.9%) trails patch aggregation, and accuracy saturates around 64 patches per image. Under an image-level split, the same configuration reaches 99.9% (+5.0 pp) and the whole-image baseline 99.2% (+7.3 pp), an inflation as large as the entire effect of patch size that also erases the differences between design choices. We recommend patches as large as possible while leaving enough to aggregate (about 512 px here), a nano backbone, and tree-level splits for bark benchmarks.

items.title: Do Search-Augmented Recommenders Use the Latest Search Episode?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a user returns to a recommendation feed after searching, does the latest search episode help rank the next item? Aggregate ranking gains leave open whether search-augmented recommenders use the latest search at prediction time or benefit from broader search state and representation learning. FocalSwap is a counterfactual audit that masks or replaces the latest episode or the full search history while holding the target, candidates, recommendation history, and trained scorer fixed. A planted-signal test and GenSAR's native search-item prediction task verify that FocalSwap detects known search dependence. In proxy analyses, KuaiSAR's routing gain falls below the shuffled threshold, and Qilin's clearest matched-search advantage appears at high taxonomy overlap. The primary comparisons for SESRec and UniSAR do not establish a positive ranking gain from the latest search episode alone. For the full search history, the estimated contribution depends on the control. On 66,139 shared instances across three UniSAR checkpoints, neutral masking consistently lowers mean reciprocal rank (RR). Replacing the history with observed searches matched on category and activity profile changes 44.1 to 44.8 percent of target ranks, yet the original history has little average advantage. In the primary assignment, matched replacements yield mean RR 0.002770 to 0.006604 higher than neutral masking across checkpoints. The adjusted intervals for this difference lie above zero under the primary assignment and all five alternative assignments per checkpoint. Search audits should specify which inputs changed and what replaced them, and report both how often ranks move and how much the original search helps.

items.title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06470v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

items.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07222v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .005. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

items.title: FisherDistill: Diffusion Distribution Distillation via Closed-Form Fisher Critics
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07604v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in diffusion distillation have enabled high-quality image generation in only one or a few network function evaluations (NFEs). Despite their efficiency, aggressively distilled generators often retain a residual distribution gap from their multi-step teachers, motivating recent methods to introduce adversarial refinement with a learned discriminator. In this work, we ask whether such refinement necessarily requires a learned adversarial discriminator. We introduce \textbf{FisherDistill}, a simple alternative based on Fisher linear discriminant analysis. Using intermediate representations from the frozen teacher, we estimate the first- and second-order statistics of real and generated samples and derive a closed-form Fisher direction that maximally separates their feature distributions relative to within-class variation. This direction provides a lightweight refinement signal that complements the original distillation objective without requiring an additional adversarial discriminator or its optimization loop. Across multiple distillation frameworks, our approach consistently improves generation quality over their respective distilled baselines and substantially closes the gap to adversarially refined counterparts. Code: https://bhosalems.github.io/FisherDistill/

items.title: SPDMX: Large-Scale Open Stem Audio From Symbolic Music
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09140v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large public datasets have driven recent progress in machine learning, from text and vision to speech and general audio. Music remains an outlier, as copyright blocks redistribution of training audio, in particular for modern tasks that need individual stems rather than mixtures. Existing multitrack resources trade off realism, scale, and licensing, as synthetic alternatives rely on proprietary VSTs or naive open rendering that yields weak stems. We introduce SPDMX, an openly-licensed stem corpus rendered from the public-domain PDMX dataset. SPDMX comprises $5{,}469$ song-hours ($2{,}734$ song-hours, or $34.8\%$, of which are multitrack scores) at $44.1$ kHz under CC BY 4.0, with paired MIDI and identifiers that link our dataset to PDMX's original metadata. To our knowledge, SPDMX's multitrack subset constitutes the largest openly-licensed synthetic multitrack subset by song-hours. We then demo SPDMX as a dataset for both source separation and transcription, showing how its increased scale can enable better training of models on synthetic data. We release SPDMX, as well as the open creation pipeline for reuse on other symbolic music datasets.

items.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09218v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. To study harness optimization in these settings, we introduce PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and investigate whether agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task. To this end, we introduce BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context. We evaluate BOXBOX on PerfRace under matched test-time budgets, comparing it with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution, and Harness Scaling. BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline.

items.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09822v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.57x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 12x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

items.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-based Management of Continuum Resources
items.summary: arXiv:2611.10292v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lilanpei/continuum-intent-compiler.

items.title: Do Benign-Trained Hidden-State Probes Detect Tool Errors Under Adversarial Conditions?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.11172v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Repeatedly training language models on their own generated data may create a synthetic-data feedback loop in which errors and distributional biases are reintroduced into subsequent training datasets. This paper studies that process in biomedical question answering (QA) using PubMedQA and two Qwen2.5 model sizes, 0.5B and 3B parameters. The study compares a recursive synthetic-data condition, in which generation G(k+1) is trained on answers produced by G(k), against a Human-Control condition that repeatedly uses the original human training data. The study evaluates across four generations from G0-G3 with two random seeds (42 and 123) and a fixed evaluation set of 1,000 expert-labeled samples. The evaluation includes disease and chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, lexical and semantic similarity, answer length, repetition rate, and other evaluation metrics. The Recursive condition for both model sizes and both seeds showed larger declines than the Human-Control condition in disease entity F1, chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, ROUGE-L, and cosine similarity. Under the fixed no-repeat 3-gram decoding constraint, the main observed behavioral change was increased answer length, while the measured 3-gram repetition rate did not increase. The magnitude of the difference-in-change was larger for the 3B model than for the 0.5B model. This difference was particularly apparent in disease F1, context-supported rate, cosine similarity, and answer length. These results show domain-specific changes associated with using recursive synthetic-data training in biomedical QA, but do not establish clinical hallucination rates or universal model collapse.

items.title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
items.summary: arXiv:2611.12412v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research typically tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and to our knowledge not with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.

items.title: MARS: Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams for Video Forgery Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.12508v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalizing deepfake detection across facial manipulation and fully generated video remains challenging due to forgery traces varying with the manipulation method and scene content. Explicit spatial and temporal feature differences offer a way to capture this variation, but also respond to natural texture and motion, motivating their joint interpretation with appearance features. We investigate whether combining multiscale feature differences with adapted appearance representations improves detection across both forgery categories. We introduce Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams (MARS), a two-path video detector. The residual path applies fixed spatial and temporal difference-of-Gaussians operators to frozen intermediate features and models the resulting differences alongside appearance context across frames. The semantic path adapts the encoder's normalization parameters for frame classification, and a clip-dependent gate combines their predictions. Under a shared protocol across seven datasets, MARS achieves the highest average AUROC of 91.43\%, outperforming seven compared detectors. When trained on facial manipulations alone, MARS achieves 93.99\% AUROC on GenVideo and 75.50\% on DF26, demonstrating transfer to generated videos without generated-video training data. MARS also provides signed patch and frame contributions, whose faithfulness we evaluate through controlled spatial and temporal removal against random controls. MARS is publicly available for research: Project page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mars/ Github: https://github.com/VectorInstitute/mars

items.title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
items.summary: arXiv:2611.12529v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sensitive to the VH's actual behaviour over the interaction.

items.title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14106v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. items.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15108v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of a claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks normalization and makes algorithmic conversion non-transitive. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($irrel : \Pi P{:}Prop.\,\Pi p,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, $\Pi$-covariant subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, compile to unification-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$), and match declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) for open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

items.title: Reframing Video Inverse Tone Mapping as Blind Posterior Inference via Latent Luminance Supervision
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15146v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-dynamic-range (HDR) displays are now common, but most video content, such as archival footage, broadcast material, and the output of generative video models, exists only in standard dynamic range (SDR). The need is sharpest for generated video, which has no HDR master at all and is graded alongside live-action and visual-effects material finished in HDR. Converting SDR to HDR means undoing a tone-mapping operation that was never recorded, and clipping destroys the radiance wherever it acts, so HDR recovery is a blind inverse problem. Methods built on generative video priors fill clipped regions with plausible structure, but their reconstructions are systematically biased: in every public method we test, saturated content leans too bright or too dark, and the direction of the lean moves with the tone operator behind the input. We call this failure the luminance error, measure both its magnitude and its sign, and make it the focus of this work. Reframing ITM as posterior inference under an unknown operator locates the failure in two places and yields two corrections. A fixed affine functional of the video-diffusion latent reads log-luminance without decoding; on that coordinate an asymmetric loss selects an expectile of the posterior, applied only where clipping leaves luminance unconstrained. We also synthesize training SDR through an explicit family of tone operators, so the model marginalizes over what the observation cannot show. Trained this way, our luminance error stays flatter across operators and smaller on average than any public method, and the full system achieves the best perceptual quality on all three benchmarks.

items.title: Vision-Grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment for Scalable Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15328v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval (TBPR) aims to retrieve individuals with texts in multiple languages. Despite its practical importance, it has been overlooked by existing research, which mainly focuses on English-only retrieval. The only prior attempt at multilingual TBPR suffers from (1) the absence of a large-scale, multilingual pretraining dataset and (2) a suboptimal model architecture for multilingual text encoding and cross-modal alignment, which employs a shared encoder that overlooks linguistic heterogeneity and relies on English as a pivot for cross-modal alignment, introducing English-centric bias. For this, we contribute MultiPedes, the first large-scale, pedestrian-centric multilingual pretraining dataset. It contains 10 million image-text pairs across four languages, constructed by a multilingual quality-aware data construction pipeline. We also propose ViSeLA (Vision-grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment), a novel framework featuring: (1) a semantic-aware multilingual learning module that extends the mixture-of-experts architecture by routing language-invariant semantics to specialized experts for improved multilingual feature learning; and (2) a vision-grounded cross-modal alignment module that employs a semantic probe to capture fine-grained semantics across modalities, enabling direct cross-modal alignment without relying on a pivot language. Extensive experiments on both multilingual and English-only TBPR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ViSeLA. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Flame-Chasers/ViSeLA

items.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16057v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

items.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16246v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models drive the robot directly from camera views, yet a VLA alone shows three typical failures. It walks past the goal, stops before reaching it, and rarely recovers after going off track. Pairing a VLA with a large language model (LLM) planner fixes these failures, but queries the LLM throughout every episode, adding token costs and latency. We introduce Harness-to-Executor (H2E), a session-level distillation method that pairs an LLM planner and a frozen VLA as a heterogeneous training agent, keeps only sessions that reach the goal, and then trains a VLA alone on them so no LLM is used at test time. In these sessions, the planner gives sub-instructions and moves the robot with its own tools, detours are common, and the planner decides when to stop. H2E therefore labels every motion as a VLA action for the original task, whoever made it. It masks the loss on steps moving away from the goal and assigns end labels to states near it, so the VLA learns where the task ends. H2E sets a new state of the art on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE. It raises an 8B VLA's success rate by 15.6% and 11.1% respectively, surpassing methods trained on 10M samples. The distilled VLA exceeds its agent on unseen episodes with zero LLM tokens and runs 3.7 times faster.

items.title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16424v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.

items.title: TAPES: Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling for Financial Diffusion Samplers
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16484v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Financial diffusion samplers are often reused with a small number of function evaluations (NFE) inside scenario and risk pipelines, where numerical time-grid error can distort terminal quantities such as covariances, tails, and drawdown proxies. We study offline grid construction for a frozen probability-flow ODE: the score network, conditioning, Euler solver, report normalization, and deployment NFE remain fixed. TAPES (Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling) estimates signed local defects by Richardson comparisons, transports them through the remaining discrete flow and a terminal-report adjoint, and optimizes the squared norm of their sum before a capped direct refinement. We show that this transported signed sum is the first-order terminal-report error and quantify, under an aligned-defect model, the inefficiency of diagonal criteria. Across six budgets on a regime-switching simulation and chronologically held-out Mag7 contexts, TAPES gives the lowest design- and audit-report errors in all 24 dataset--budget--report rows within the reported five-pipeline panel. Cross-budget mean relative audit-error reductions are about 10--11% on Regime-SV and about 1% on Mag7, with Bonferroni intervals excluding zero; all displayed winners persist under a doubled-resolution reference, and a small Regime-SV Heun probe preserves the TAPES-first audit ordering. TAPES changes only the offline schedule and retains the prescribed deployment NFE; claims concern numerical fidelity to frozen generators.

items.title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16748v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

items.title: Beyond Answering: Learning to Speak First and Act in Streaming Video
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17048v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) lets the model act on what it sees by invoking external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporating returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities.

items.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17110v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

items.title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17442v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How do action budgets shape vision-language navigation (VLN) exploration, and what expert supervision best teaches budget-aware search? We study budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within a budget, with discovery defined geometrically by camera field of view and proximity. Distinct discoveries provide a denser evaluation signal than single-target success. We cast expert design as a choice of scene abstraction: a single budget-indexed Bellman recursion, applied to different abstractions of the full environment, yields experts that differ in what they know. An object-level Bellman expert is given every target location and reduces search to budgeted routing. A room-level Bellman expert retains observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors but withholds the contents of unexplored rooms, so it must search for targets that its student also cannot see. We distill both experts into Uni-NaVid under matched training conditions and also evaluate greedy-frontier supervision on held-out HM3D scenes. Changing only the stated budget changes learned trajectories. Despite higher object-level expert return, room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection among evaluated VLNs at every tested budget. At 2000 steps, it finds 72.7% of reachable targets, versus 68.5% under greedy-frontier supervision, 65.5% under object-level supervision, and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results show that expert-return rankings need not predict supervision quality for VLN exploration, and motivate choosing an expert's abstraction with the student's information in mind rather than by expert return alone.

items.title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17466v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

items.title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Object Tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses a CARLA autonomous driving simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA) and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

items.title: A Generalizable Approach to Safety-Aware Robotic Behavior Planning with an Explicit Constraint Space
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18026v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.

items.title: Eco3R: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18099v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame self-attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames under a fixed computational budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be selected independently of video content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a small number of uniformly sampled frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present Eco3R, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). Eco3R ($\pi^3$) matches $\pi^3$'s success rate on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos while running 13.8 times faster. With refocusing, Eco3R (VGGT) raises VGGT's success rate from 70% to 82% while running 8.5 times faster on 500 frames. Eco3R can reconstruct sequences of up to 4,000 frames on a single A100 GPU, while Eco3R ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 fps, achieving the lowest online absolute trajectory error.

items.title: OpenAI’s Astra Is a Boon to Robotics, Says Nvidia Robotics Chief Deepu Talla
items.summary:
When OpenAI released its Astra model in September, users quickly found that it excelled at tasks that require understanding the physical world. One of those most impressed by its performance was Nvidia’s robotics chief Deepu Talla, who told The Information it is a breakthrough in efforts to create robots that can handle a wide variety of jobs.

Astra has made it 100 times faster to create some kinds of data for training robotic AI models and could help automate the process of putting robots to work in factories, Talla said on the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode, which was recorded before Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO, is available here.)

items.title: Nvidia’s Board Should Come Clean on Huang’s Resignation
items.summary:
Memo to the board of Nvidia: Folks, you need to explain why you pressured Jensen Huang to resign. Otherwise, a bring-back-Jensen movement will only grow and could theoretically escalate to the point where it threatens your roles on Nvidia’s board. Even President Donald Trump has weighed in, supporting Huang. The board could use Nvidia’s earnings update on Tuesday to provide everyone with some answers.

As quixotic as the Jensen loyalists’ effort may seem right now, some of their complaints are on the money. A letter from investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker posted on X on Friday, for instance, made the point that there was “massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding” Huang’s departure. The pair were correct to say that a “slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia” was in everyone’s best interests.

items.title: Google DeepMind Strategy Chief Jasjeet Sekhon Departs for Anthropic
items.summary:

items.title: PwC on where AI can help drive revenue
items.summary:
Until recently, AI adoption was the watchword in executive circles. Lately, the conversation has shifted from how companies can use AI to drive productivity to how they leverage it to drive growth and new revenue streams As the technology reshapes existing business models, executives are exploring new ways to make money from their data, develop new products and services, and rethink how their organizations operate.

Rima Safari, U.S. data, analytics and AI practice leader at PwC US, helps the world’s largest organizations move from AI experimentation to business outcomes. The Information’s founder and editor in chief Jessica Lessin sat down with Safari to examine the opportunities and challenges facing companies as they transform their businesses.

Unearthing Revenue Channels

Safari identified two ways companies are relying on AI to drive growth. The first is using AI to analyze how existing processes and data can lead to new insights, which they can turn into new products and services to sell externally. She cited an aerospace and defense company—a PwC client—that used AI to analyze more than 30 years of airplane maintenance records, including millions of handwritten documents, in a short time frame. The company saw an opportunity to turn the findings into a product for other airlines that could help them better manage inventory and maintenance.

“It’s one example of how companies are asking questions around how they can reimagine their businesses,” she said. “A lot of companies are looking at how they can leverage insights to help drive revenue growth.”

The example also points to a second opportunity: using proprietary and contextually relevant data to deliver timely insights for key business decisions. Safari compared it to GPS navigation software, which uses live traffic data to recommend the best route.

“It’s contextually relevant information at the right point in time that allows you to immediately make a decision. That is what organizations need in this agentic world,” Safari said. As companies gain access to increasingly similar frontier models, their proprietary data and ability to put it to work will become a more important source of competitive advantage.

That makes protecting the data essential, she said.

True AI Transformation Starts With a Blank Whiteboard, Not Yesterday’s Blueprint

That sort of reimagination and transformative thinking is difficult for large enterprises, many of which have spent decades building entrenched processes. While startups are often quicker to rethink how work gets done, Safari said, established companies often fall into the trap of treating AI as another efficiency tool, asking how to automate parts of a process.

“That should not be the question at all,” she said. “It should be: With AI, how do I reimagine this entire process?”

Rethinking Security

One very important thing companies need to rethink from a risk perspective is their security measures, which have come into sharper focus as AI agents move beyond controlled environments and start to act more independently in real-world systems. Safari said these risks have slowed adoption but are also changing how companies approach AI development.

“Historically, organizations often prioritized experimentation and rapid development, with the expectation that security and governance could be addressed as solutions matured and scaled. That mindset is fundamentally shifting. Security can no longer be an afterthought—it needs to be embedded into the architecture and design of AI solutions from day one,” Safari said.

Traditional security protocols were designed around human users, Safari noted, not the large number of agents now deployed.

“As AI fundamentally transforms how enterprises operate, security frameworks must evolve alongside it. We need to rethink how we establish trust, manage access and govern an increasingly autonomous digital workforce,” she said.

Tokenomics and the Changing Workforce

Tokenomics has become a recurring concern for executives, Safari said. Companies that once celebrated AI usage through internal leaderboards are now scrutinizing spending.

“You don’t want to use the most sophisticated models for something as simple as summarizing a document,” she said. Instead, companies are increasingly embracing a more diverse AI ecosystem with a fit-for-purpose strategy, strategically combining frontier models with open-weight and open-source alternatives to optimize for performance, cost, control and the unique requirements of each workload.

On the workforce. Safari expects the emphasis to be on upskilling and reskilling rather than simply doing more with fewer people. As agents take on a growing share of tasks, she said employees will increasingly be responsible for orchestrating workflows involving both human colleagues and AI. Just as organizations’ data will be a competitive advantage, so too will employees who have the skills to build on that data. Safari expects technical fluency to become essential at every level of the organizational chart, including at the executive level.

“I say every executive will need to become a builder in some capacity—not necessarily a technologist, but someone with the technical fluency to turn ideas into solutions and actively shape how their business operates,” she said.

items.title: Microsoft Data Shows Claude Is Stalling Against Copilot in Office
items.summary:
Anthropic’s latest push into enterprise apps rattled Microsoft investors last week. Microsoft’s own internal data paints a less threatening picture, at least so far.

Usage of Anthropic features that allow people to do work inside Microsoft’s Office apps with Claude, such as sorting email or generating slide decks, has been falling further behind usage of Microsoft’s Copilot in recent months, according to internal Microsoft data described by an employee with knowledge of it. The number of weekly users of those features, known as Claude for Microsoft 365, is less than one-tenth the number of weekly users of the paid version of Copilot, Microsoft’s own AI tools, in Office, which has been growing at a much faster rate, the person said.
