items.title: The Controversial AI Interpretability Research that Caught Sam Altman’s Eye
items.summary:
During OpenAI’s talks in recent months with AI startup Goodfire over a possible acquisition or partnership—discussions my colleagues and I reported this morning—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was particularly interested in the work of Nick Cammarata, a onetime OpenAI researcher now at Goodfire who has made waves recently with new claims about how AI thinks.

Cammarata published an essay last month and a follow-up report last week that have caused quite a stir among AI researchers—with some applauding it as a potential breakthrough in our ability to understand AI models and others dismissing it as hype. The reaction goes to show that some areas of AI research are still so immature that scientists don’t even agree on what counts as good research—a fact that hasn’t prevented billion-dollar valuations for startups based on unproven AI technology. 

Goodfire’s research specialty is known as mechanistic interpretability, or mech interp for short, which seeks to understand the inner workings of AI models rather than just their outward behavior. AI models are made of trillions of numbers, making them “black boxes” that a person can’t understand the way a programmer can simply read the lines of code in traditional software. As a result, it’s tricky to know how an AI model will act in new situations and to understand mistakes when they occur.

items.title: OpenAI Explored $5 Billion–Plus Acquisition of Startup That Decodes How AI ‘Thinks’
items.summary:
As OpenAI staff this summer scrambled to understand how its AI caused security breaches inside and outside the company, leaders including CEO Sam Altman spoke multiple times with Goodfire, an Anthropic-backed startup whose technology aims to figure out why AI models behave the way they do and how to prevent them from going rogue.

At one point, a senior OpenAI executive floated the idea of buying the two-year-old startup for more than $5 billion or forming another kind of business partnership, according to two people familiar with the proposal. That price would have represented a steep premium to Goodfire’s private valuation of $1.25 billion in a financing it announced in February.

items.title: Nvidia’s Earnings on Deck; Anthropic’s Public Debut
items.summary:
If life was simple, the biggest question this week for people in tech would be where Anthropic shares open when the AI firm goes public. (Above $150 a share? See below.) Instead, we can’t rule out that more news breaks in the Nvidia drama and overwhelms Anthropic’s week in the sun. That news could be anything from reports of other women who had affairs with the now-departed CEO, Jensen Huang to developments in the campaign to bring him back. Huang, meanwhile, has agreed to testify before Congress, which could happen this week.

Of course, even without such developments, Nvidia will be in the news. The AI chip designer on Tuesday is scheduled to report earnings for its third fiscal quarter, ending in late October. Those earnings will remind us all of why it is such a star company: It has projected revenue growth of around 89%, continuing a reacceleration of growth this fiscal year from last year’s “slowdown” (when revenue grew 66%). What we’ll be focused on more than the numbers will be comments from Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress. While as finance chief she’s a fixture on these calls, on Tuesday she makes her first public appearance in charge of the company since Huang’s exit.

items.title: How a Chinese Energy Company Is Outpacing the U.S. on AI Power Technology
items.summary:
Ulanqab, a city in China’s Inner Mongolia region, used to be known for its potatoes. Now it’s where a Chinese renewable energy firm is trying out a new way to plug in AI chips that shows China’s edge in the power systems that data centers need.

Envision Energy has started using an 800-volt direct-current system to power computing workloads at its data center there, the Shanghai-based company said earlier this month. The setup, which wastes less electricity between the grid and the chips, is widely expected to become the standard way to power increasingly energy-hungry AI servers, and Envision says it is the first to run it in a functioning data center. Nvidia and its partners are still preparing the same kind of system for their next generation of AI hardware, due next year.
